Fact.Name: Months disabled or in school
Fact.Description:
The number of months the filer was either disabled or in school in the current tax year.
THE CONFLATION IN THIS FACT'S NAME IS THE PRINTED SHAPE, NOT A MODELLING SHORTCUT — decided from the printed instruments rather than argued from the graph, and recorded HERE because this declaration is where four lanes' worth of "split it by limb" proposals land. THE QUESTION PUT: does any printed instrument ask a student-months figure and a disabled-months figure SEPARATELY, or does it ask one count for the disjunction? THE ANSWER IS ONE COUNT, in every instrument that asks at all: - Form 2441 asks NO months figure anywhere. Line 5 says only "If married filing jointly, enter your spouse's earned income (if you or your spouse was a student or was disabled, see the instructions)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1), and the line B checkbox is itself the disjunction: "If you or your spouse was a student or was disabled during 2025" (lines 15-16). The months are an instruction-level quantity the form never collects, which is why this writable is off-form to begin with. - The instructions ask the disjunction per month, twice, once per chain: "For each month or part of a month your spouse was a student or was disabled, they are considered to have worked and earned income" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4) and "For each month or part of a month you were a student or disabled, your earned income is considered to be at least $250" (lines 265-268). - Pub. 503 is the one instrument that ENUMERATES the two limbs, and it still asks one count over them: "Your spouse is treated as having earned income for any month that they are: 1. A full-time student, or 2. Physically or mentally not able to care for themselves" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 4), and in the Earned Income Limit section "Your spouse who is either a full-time student or not able to care for themselves is treated as having earned income. Their earned income for each month is considered to be at least $250" (lines 750-753). - The statute's per-month test is likewise a single disjunction: the spouse is "deemed for each month during which such spouse is a full-time student at an educational institution, or is such a qualifying individual, to be gainfully employed and to have earned income of not less than" $250 or $500 (26 U.S.C. 21, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section21&num=0&edition=2024). - AND THE PRINTED ALGORITHM IS UNROLLED IN A WORKED EXAMPLE, which is the strongest form this answer takes. Pub. 503's Jim and Sharon example states one fact about Sharon, that she "isn't able to care for herself for 11 months during the tax year" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 12), and its printed limit table computes her deemed income on line 3 as that ONE count times the rate, 11 times $250 = $2,750 (lines 808-809). One count, one multiplication. No printed worksheet decomposes it.
WHAT THAT DECIDES, AND IT IS NOT THE SAME AS "THE SPLIT IS IMPOSSIBLE". The printed RULE is per-limb and the printed DATUM is not, and that asymmetry is the whole finding. Section 21(b)(1)(C)'s abode condition rides on the disabled limb alone — Pub. 503 attaches "(Your spouse must also live with you for more than half the year.)" to its item 2 and not its item 1 (lines 268-269) — so a filer who is BOTH a student and disabled and fails the abode test should deem on their STUDENT months only, and this Int cannot say how many of its months those were. That residual is therefore IRREDUCIBLE FROM ANSWERED INPUTS rather than merely unbuilt: no printed instrument collects the datum that would resolve it. It is contained by cdcc:/knockoutStudentOrDisabled and witnessed by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-both-limbs-abode-failed-residual.
THE SPLIT IS COSTED HERE SO NOBODY RE-INVENTS IT, which is this dictionary's own derivation and the reason the finding is worth more than a verdict line. A naive per-limb pair of counts DOES NOT RECONSTRUCT what this Int means and would be a regression, not a refinement: a filer who is a student January to June and disabled July to December answers six and six for a union of twelve, and a filer who is both a student and disabled for the same six months answers six and six for a union of six. Same two answers, different truth, so the deemed months are not a function of the pair. The only honest per-limb shape is a PARTITION — "months as a full-time student" plus "months not able to care for yourself AND not a full-time student" — whose second question no printed instruction poses and which a taxpayer working from the printed text would not produce. Its blast radius is not small either, and the figure is counted directly rather than estimated: this path carries 26 <Dependency> reads outside its own declaration — 16 in dictionary/ty2025/cdcc.xml and 10 in dictionary/ty2025/income.xml — including the overlap machinery (cdcc:/cdccMonthsBothSpousesStudentOrDisabled, the arithmetic check that the two per-filer counts sum to at most twelve, and cdcc:/cdccOverlappedMonthsAllocatedToPrimaryFiler with its validity proof), every one of which a partition multiplies.
THE RESIDUAL WAS A DISCLOSED DEVIATION ON THE THEN-PRINTED INTAKE, closed by decision rather than by a new printed instrument: /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent and /filers/*/cdccMonthsUnableToCareForSelfAndNotStudent below model the partition as an off-form attestation, the way cdcc:/cdccOverlappedMonthsAllocatedToPrimaryFiler already models the taxpayer's own allocation choice, on the project owner's ruling that the writables ARE the question surface — "Service flow only exists if there are writables to fill. It doesn't have tax knowledge" — so an off-form attestation is this dictionary's to declare, and the printed text's silence is not a veto. The conflated count above is ITSELF off-form by this same finding ("Form 2441 asks NO months figure anywhere"), so the printed text never authorised the question this dictionary already asks either. This writable is NOT retired or retyped: the partition is additive and its consumers fall back here, so every one of the 26 Dependency reads counted above keeps working unchanged. THE MEASUREMENT, taken directly rather than inherited: scenarios/ holds 896 JSON files of which 731 carry a top-level "facts" store, and 0 of those 731 answer this path. Positive controls on the identical scan, taken before the zero was accepted: 728 isStudent, 728 isDisabled, 730 /filers/, 704 formW2s, 686 cdccCareProviders, 696 livedTogetherAllYearWithSpouse, 30 spouseLivedTogetherMonths, 10 writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount.

Fact.Name: Months the filer was a full-time student (CDCC deemed income, student limb)
Fact.Description:
The number of months, or parts of months, the filer was a full-time student at an educational institution during the tax year, including months they were also unable to care for themself. THE STUDENT HALF OF THE PARTITION that /filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool conflates.
WHY THIS IS SEPARATE FROM THE DISABLED HALF, which is the whole reason the partition exists: section 21(d)(2) deems a month in which the filer "is a full-time student at an educational institution, OR is such a qualifying individual" (26 U.S.C. 21, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section21&num=0&edition=2024), and "such a qualifying individual" points at section 21(b)(1)(C), which additionally requires sharing the taxpayer's abode for more than half the year. So a STUDENT month deems with NO abode test and a DISABLED month deems only behind one. Pub. 503 prints the same asymmetry, attaching "(Your spouse must also live with you for more than half the year.)" to its item 2 and not its item 1 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 4). A single count cannot carry it.
A MONTH IN WHICH THE FILER WAS BOTH A STUDENT AND UNABLE TO CARE FOR THEMSELF BELONGS HERE, not in the twin, and that is a deliberate ordering rather than a tie-break: the statute's test is a disjunction, so such a month deems on the student limb regardless of the abode test, and counting it here is what makes the abode gate apply to the twin ALONE. The twin's own definition carries the matching exclusion, so the two counts PARTITION the qualifying months and can be added without double-counting.
BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PROMISED: this fact is ADDITIVE. The conflated writable above is neither retyped nor removed, and its 26 existing Dependency reads keep working unchanged. Consumers PREFER this partition and FALL BACK to the conflated count when it is unanswered — the same idiom already used for /primaryFilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation in this same chain.

Fact.Name: Filer meets the section 21(e)(7) five month full time student test
Fact.Description:
Whether this filer is a "student" as section 21(e)(7) defines the word for the child and dependent care credit: an individual who, during EACH OF 5 CALENDAR MONTHS of the taxable year, is a full-time student at an educational organization. The per-limb month count /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent is the datum and 5 is the floor.
WHY THE DEFINITION HAS TO BE WIRED AND NOT ASSUMED. Section 21(d)(2) deems earned income for each month a spouse "is a full-time student at an educational institution, or is such a qualifying individual", and the word "student" in that disjunction is a DEFINED term: 21(e)(7) supplies it, and the definition has a floor the deeming sentence itself never states. Without this test the graph deems on the student limb from the FIRST answered month, so a filer enrolled full-time for one month reaches the same machinery as one enrolled for nine.
THE POSTURE IS PERMISSIVE-UNTIL-ANSWERED, deliberately. The count is read IsComplete-first and this fact resolves TRUE whenever the count is unanswered, so a return that has never been asked the per-limb question keeps exactly the behaviour it had before this fact existed; only an ANSWERED count below 5 makes it FALSE. The count is an off-form attestation (no printed instrument collects it, a finding recorded in full on /filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool), so reading its silence as a definite "fewer than 5 months" would newly refuse the whole answered-isStudent population on a question the application does not yet ask. Complete-safe by construction: Not over an All whose first conjunct is an IsComplete, so it never resolves Incomplete.
WHAT IT GATES TODAY: the student limb of /filers/*/isStudentOrDisabled. It does NOT yet gate the deemed-months arithmetic, which reads /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent directly from income.xml; /filers/*/cdccQualifyingStudentMonths below is the capped, gated count that arithmetic should read instead.

Fact.Name: The answered full time student month count is admissible
Fact.Description:
Whether the answered /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent is a count one taxable year can carry: at least 0 and at most 12. Section 21(e)(7) counts "calendar months during the taxable year", and a taxable year holds twelve of them, so 13 is not a small overstatement but an impossible answer.
WHY A DERIVED GUARD AND NOT ONLY THE WRITABLE'S LIMIT. The Limit type="Min"/"Max" pair now on that writable enforces the same bound ONLY at JVM validation time (a Limit on a Writable fires as a validation Error, gov.irs.factgraph.limits.Min and .Max, and NEVER at resolution); on the default engine an out-of-bound count is not refused at all and resolves normally. So the Limit alone cannot stop a wrong number, and this derived fact is the value-level guard the counted facts route through. It is the same pairing /familyAndHousehold/*/dateOfBirth carries with /familyAndHousehold/*/dateOfBirthAdmissible, and it is deliberately modelled on it.
COMPLETE-SAFE AND PERMISSIVE WHEN UNANSWERED: an unanswered count is not an inadmissible one, so this resolves TRUE and nothing downstream is refused for a question never asked.

Fact.Name: The answered disabled-limb month count is admissible
Fact.Description: Whether the answered /filers/*/cdccMonthsUnableToCareForSelfAndNotStudent is a count one tax year can carry: at least 0 and at most 12 months or parts of months. The Writable Limit on that count enforces this only during JVM validation, not at fact resolution, so this complete-safe value-level twin is needed anywhere the answered count feeds deemed-income arithmetic. If the count is unanswered this resolves true; an unanswered off-form attestation is not an inadmissible answer.

Fact.Name: Months this filer qualifies as a section 21 student
Fact.Description:
The full-time-student month count AFTER the section 21(e)(7) definition and the twelve month ceiling are applied: the answered count when the filer is a 21(e)(7) student and the count is admissible, 0 when the filer answered a count below the five month floor, and Incomplete when the count is unanswered or inadmissible.
THIS IS THE COUNT THE DEEMED INCOME ARITHMETIC MULTIPLIES when the per-limb partition is answered. income:/{primary,secondary}FilerCdccQualifyingMonths reads it for the student term; the pre-partition conflated count remains the documented fallback when either limb count is unanswered.
INCOMPLETE, NOT ZERO, ON A COUNT NEVER ANSWERED. The Switch has no default arm on purpose: a return that has not answered the per-limb partition has no student-month figure at all, and a silent 0 would be a number this dictionary invented. Consumers that must keep working on the conflated pre-partition count read /filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool behind their own IsComplete gate, exactly as income.xml does when the per-limb partition is unanswered.

Fact.Name: Months the filer was unable to care for themself and was not a full-time student (CDCC deemed income, disabled limb)
Fact.Description:
The number of months, or parts of months, the filer was physically or mentally incapable of caring for themself AND was NOT also a full-time student that month. THE DISABLED HALF OF THE PARTITION, and the exclusion in its name is load-bearing.
THE EXCLUSION IS WHAT MAKES THIS COUNT DISJOINT FROM THE STUDENT COUNT. The full-time- student count includes months also disabled; this count excludes those months, and a third overlap count records them separately. The deemed union uses student months when the five-month definition passes, and disabled-only plus overlap months when it fails. This keeps a both-limbs month from being lost for a short-term student or counted twice for a qualifying student. ANY QUESTION WORDING THAT DROPS THE "and were not also a full-time student that month" CLAUSE silently folds the overlap into this count and can double-count.
THIS COUNT IS THE ONE THE ABODE TEST GATES. Section 21(b)(1)(C) makes an incapable spouse a qualifying individual only if they share the taxpayer's principal abode for more than half the year, so these months deem only when filers:/filers/*/cdccQualifyingPerson holds; the student twin's months deem unconditionally. That gate is ANNUAL, not per month, so it stays one existing question rather than twelve new ones.
ADDITIVE, with the same fallback contract as its twin: the conflated writable above is untouched and consumers fall back to it while this partition is unanswered.

Fact.Name: Months the filer was unable to care for themself and was a full-time student (CDCC deemed income, overlap limb)
Fact.Description: The number of months, or parts of months, the filer was physically or mentally incapable of caring for themself AND was also a full-time student at an educational institution. This overlap is already included in /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent and is excluded from /filers/*/cdccMonthsUnableToCareForSelfAndNotStudent. It is reassigned to the disabled limb only when the positive student count fails section 21(e)(7)'s five-month definition, and it is admitted only behind /filers/*/cdccQualifyingPerson's section 21(b)(1)(C) abode test. When the student definition passes, the student term already counts it and this overlap term is zero, preventing double counting.

Fact.Name: The answered disabled-student overlap count is admissible
Fact.Description: Whether the answered /filers/*/cdccMonthsUnableToCareForSelfAndStudent is a count one tax year can carry: at least 0 and at most 12 months or parts of months. The Writable Limit enforces that only during JVM validation, not fact resolution. If the count is unanswered this resolves true; an unanswered off-form attestation is not an inadmissible answer. It also cannot exceed /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent, because it is a subset of that count. This relationship is value-guarded because Writable Limits do not run at fact resolution.

Fact.Name: The answered disjoint student and disabled-only month counts fit one tax year
Fact.Description: Whether /filers/*/cdccMonthsAsFullTimeStudent plus /filers/*/cdccMonthsUnableToCareForSelfAndNotStudent is at most 12 months or parts of months. The counts are disjoint by definition, so their sum cannot exceed the twelve-month tax year. This complete-safe guard is true until both counts are answered and false only when their answered sum exceeds 12. It is consumed only behind the qualifying-person abode gate, where the disabled-only term contributes to deemed months.

Fact.Name: Filer earned more than the deemed monthly rate in at least one qualifying month
Fact.Description:
Whether, in ANY SINGLE ONE of the months this filer was a full-time student or was unable to care for themself, they earned more than the section 21(d)(2) deemed rate ($250, or $500 where two or more qualifying persons were cared for). A screening question, and the polarity is the point.
WHY THIS QUESTION AND NOT THE ONE WE ASK TODAY. cdcc:/{primary,secondary}FilerMadeLessThanDisabledOrStudentMonthlyIncome asks whether the filer made LESS than the deemed amount — a comparison against a figure no screen has told them, reaching a conclusion rather than reporting a fact, and its only consumer is a refusal. This is its mirror, and the mirror is the useful half: section 21(d)(2) says the deemed amount is a FLOOR ("earned income of not less than"), so a month at or below the rate contributes exactly the rate and needs no further detail. It is only a month ABOVE the rate that needs its own number. So a FALSE here makes the year's figure computable in closed form, and a TRUE is the only case that needs per-month amounts at all.
UNANSWERED IS NOT FALSE. Consumers require IsComplete before taking the exact path and fall back to the pre-stage computation otherwise, so leaving this unanswered preserves every existing value.

Fact.Name: Filer's earned income during the months they were a student or unable to care for themself
Fact.Description:
How much of this filer's earned income for the year was earned DURING the months they were a full-time student or unable to care for themself. The one additional number that makes the year's figure exact, and the reason it is needed is worth stating because a first draft of this stage's spec omitted it and would have shipped a defect.
THE ARITHMETIC. Correct Form 2441 line 4/5 is the sum over qualifying months of max(rate, that month's actual), PLUS the sum over the remaining months of actual. When /filers/*/cdccEarnedOverDeemedRateInAnyQualifyingMonth is FALSE, every qualifying month's actual is at or below the rate, so the first sum collapses to months x rate. The SECOND sum does not collapse — it is real money earned outside those months — and it equals the year's earned income minus THIS figure. So exact = (qualifying months x rate) + (annual earned income - this fact) and without this fact the computation silently reverts to the annual-versus-monthly under-statement it is meant to close.
WHY IT IS ANSWERABLE. It asks the filer to total what they earned inside a set of months they have already told us about. It is not a tax conclusion, needs no rate lookup, and is one number rather than twelve.
A FILER WHO EARNED NOTHING WHILE A STUDENT ANSWERS ZERO, which is the common case and the one where the whole year's figure is months x rate plus their full earnings.

Fact.Name: How many qualifying months the filer earned more than the deemed rate in
Fact.Description:
Of the months this filer was a full-time student or unable to care for themself, the number in which they earned MORE than the section 21(d)(2) deemed rate ($250, or $500 where two or more qualifying persons were cared for). Asked only when /filers/*/cdccEarnedOverDeemedRateInAnyQualifyingMonth is true; zero otherwise.
THIS FACT AND ITS DOLLAR TWIN REPLACE TWELVE PER-MONTH AMOUNTS, and the reason is arithmetic rather than convenience. The printed rule needs the sum over qualifying months of max(rate, that month's actual). Every month at or below the rate contributes exactly the rate; every month above it contributes its own amount. So with K months over the rate and E_K earned in exactly those months, the sum is E_K + (N - K) x rate — EXACTLY, for any monthly pattern, with no attribution assumed. Verified over 20,000 randomised month vectors before this fact was written.
WHAT MAKES IT ANSWERABLE, which is the test every writable in this cluster has to pass: the filer counts months and totals wages for those months. No rate arithmetic, no subtraction against a figure we have not shown them, no tax conclusion.

Fact.Name: Filer's earned income in the qualifying months that exceeded the deemed rate
Fact.Description:
The total this filer earned in exactly the months counted by /filers/*/cdccQualifyingMonthsOverDeemedRate — the qualifying months in which their actual earned income exceeded the deemed rate. The E_K term of the identity stated on that fact.
A SUBSET OF, NOT A SIBLING TO, /filers/*/cdccEarnedIncomeDuringQualifyingMonths. That fact is everything earned across ALL qualifying months; this one is the part earned in the over-rate subset. Both are needed and neither derives the other: the first supplies the earnings that must be REMOVED from the annual figure so the non-qualifying months are not double-counted, and this one supplies the amount those over-rate months contribute in place of the floor.

Fact.Name: Age 65 or older
Fact.Description:
Whether the filer is 65 or older. Pub 554 states "You are considered age 65 at the end of the year if your 65th birthday is on or before January 1 of the following year" so we include the January 1 exception here.
Do NOT use this fact for EITC calculations. That age 65 requirement does _not_ have the January 1 exception.
A FILER WHO DIED DURING THE YEAR IS AGED AS OF THE DATE OF DEATH, not as of December 31, and that is what the first two Switch arms carry. Section 63(f)(1) allows the additional amount only to a taxpayer who "has attained age 65 before the close of his taxable year", and a decedent's taxable year closes at death, so a filer who died before reaching their deemed-65 date never attained 65 within it. Without the arms this fact read a bare end-of-year comparison and granted the additional standard deduction, Schedule R Part I qualification and the elderly/disabled credit to a decedent who never reached the age.
The spouse arm reuses /MFJDeceasedSpouseReachedAge65ForStandardD rather than re-deriving the comparison, and the taxpayer arm reads /primaryFilerAgeDayBeforeDeath, its twin. Both arms are gated so that a return with no death answered falls through to the end-of-year comparison unchanged. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (Form 540, Form 540NR).

This is explicitly different than the rule for turning 65 (the maximum age for EITC without QCs), which occurs on the person's birthday, not the day after. Because the tax code is silly.

Fact.Description:

QUESTION TEXT: "Was your Social Security number issued after the due date of your 2025 return (including extensions)?" (for the spouse: "Was your spouse's ...")
HELP TEXT: Answer Yes only if the Social Security Administration issued the number after the return's due date - for example, you are filing late or amending, and the number arrived after the deadline. If the number was issued by the due date, or you are filing on time, answer No. If you answer Yes, you cannot claim the earned income credit for 2025 on an original or an amended return.

Fact.Name: Standard deduction zeroed because an MFS filer's spouse itemizes
Fact.Description:
True when this return is married-filing-separately and the other spouse itemizes deductions on their own separate return. IRC 63(c)(6)(A) answers that case by setting THIS return's standard deduction to ZERO, not by refusing the return, and standardDeduction:/standardDeduction reads this fact as its first Switch arm.
REPLACES /spouseItemizesKnockout, whose body was All(/spouseItemizes, /MFSSpouseFilingReturnDerived) and NEVER CHECKED THE FILING STATUS AT ALL — its own Description said it "includes both facts to be defensive to edits", so the MFS-ness was carried by flow discipline rather than by the fact. That was survivable while the fact only blocked submission; it is not survivable now, because this fact CHANGES A NUMBER and a mis-fire here is silent where the knockout's was loud. The status is therefore stated.
/isFilingStatusMFS, NOT filingStatus:/treatAsMFS. treatAsMFS is the mid-interview INTENT fact — true for a taxpayer who is merely ELIGIBLE for MFS and has not yet declared a status — and gating on it would zero the standard deduction of someone who goes on to file MFJ. 63(c)(6)(A) is about "a married individual filing a separate return", i.e. the status actually filed.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE FOR NON-MFS RETURNS ONLY. THE UNANSWERED-MFS CASE IS NOT A REGRESSION IN APPEARANCE ONLY: comparing it against the retired /spouseItemizesKnockout compares against a KNOCKOUT (a submission block a filer could not silently pass), while this fact CHANGES A NUMBER a filer could otherwise silently keep. The two do not have the same safe default. FIFTEEN of the thirty committed MFS scenarios leave /spouseItemizes UNANSWERED; each resolves Incomplete here rather than Complete false.
THE RULE NOW: a NON-MFS return (isFilingStatusMFS Incomplete or Complete false) still resolves Complete FALSE — that half is untouched, and every non-MFS scenario in this repo stays byte-identical, because /isFilingStatusMFS is itself complete-safe false. An MFS return (isFilingStatusMFS Complete true) must have /spouseItemizes AND /MFSSpouseFilingReturnDerived ANSWERED before this fact resolves at all — if either is unanswered, THIS FACT IS INCOMPLETE, which standardDeduction:/standardDeduction's raw (unwrapped) Dependency on this fact turns into a genuine data-completeness refusal: /standardDeduction, /taxableIncome and /totalTax all go Incomplete rather than silently keeping the full deduction. Answered false → the All resolves false → full deduction stands, byte-identical to before. Answered true → the All resolves true → §63(c)(6)(A)'s zero, byte-identical to before. NAMED GAP, NARROWED RATHER THAN CLOSED: a short-period §63(c)(6)(C) return and a dual-status alien are unaffected arms of the same Switch on /standardDeduction, not this fact's business. The residue this fact still cannot close is the same one BlockSubmissionOnTrue always leaves standing on any refusal: the filer must answer to proceed, and no computation can supply the answer for them — but "proceed silently with a $0-cost wrong answer" is no longer that residue's shape.

Answer YES if one has already been appointed, or if you know one will be appointed before the due date of this return. Answer NO if none has been appointed and none is expected.
HELP TEXT: A surviving spouse may sign a joint return for themself and a spouse who died during the year only while no personal representative has been appointed. If a court has appointed one, the joint return with respect to the spouse who died is the personal representative's to make. Section 6013(a)(3) also lets a personal representative appointed LATER disaffirm a joint return the survivor already filed, within one year of the due date (IRC 6013(a)(3), 26 U.S.C. 6013, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section6013&num=0&edition=2024), which is why the question asks about an expected appointment and not only a completed one.
ASKED WHEN: /inScopeDeceasedSpouse holds, i.e. a married-filing-jointly return on which the spouse died during the tax year, or in the following year before this return is filed. It is asked of no other return.
UNANSWERED POSTURE, and it is the opposite of this module's usual one, deliberately: UNANSWERED READS AS "NO" AND CHANGES NOTHING. /deceasedSpouseJointReturnAuthorityDenied below reads this IsComplete-first and resolves a definite FALSE when it is blank, so a return that never sees this screen behaves exactly as it did before the question existed. The alternative, refusing every surviving-spouse joint return until the question is answered, would newly refuse a population that files correctly today, on a screen the application has not built yet. The defect this closes is an AUTHORITY defect, not a dollar defect: no figure on the return is wrong either way.
VALIDATION: Boolean, a yes/no radio pair. No Min or Max.
WHAT IT FEEDS: /deceasedSpouseJointReturnAuthorityDenied, and through it /flowKnockoutDeceasedSpouseJointReturnReservedToExecutor.

Fact.Name: A return for the tax year has already been made for the deceased spouse
Fact.Description:
SCREEN QUESTION: "Has a separate tax return for this year already been filed for your spouse?"
HELP TEXT: A surviving spouse may make the joint return only if no return for the year has already been made by the person who died (IRC 6013(a)(3), 26 U.S.C. 6013, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section6013&num=0&edition=2024). If one has, the joint return is no longer the survivor's to make.
WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE QUESTION FROM THE EXECUTOR ONE. Section 6013(a)(3) states THREE conditions, not one: no return already made by the decedent, no personal representative already appointed, and none appointed before the survivor's filing deadline. /writableDeceasedSpouseJointReturnMadeByPersonalRepresentative names the second and third; this fact carries the FIRST, which is independent of them (a decedent can have filed a separate return early in the year with no representative ever appointed).
ASKED WHEN: /inScopeDeceasedSpouse holds. UNANSWERED POSTURE: reads as "no" and changes nothing, for the reason given on the sibling writable above.
VALIDATION: Boolean, a yes/no radio pair. No Min or Max.
WHAT IT FEEDS: /deceasedSpouseJointReturnAuthorityDenied.

Fact.Name: Section 6013(a)(3) reserves this joint return to the decedent's representative
Fact.Description:
TRUE when the surviving spouse has answered away their own authority to make the joint return: either a personal representative has been or will be appointed, or a return for the year has already been made for the decedent. Section 6013(a)(3) makes the joint return "only" the representative's in either case.
COMPLETE-SAFE AND PERMISSIVE BY CONSTRUCTION. Each leg is All(IsComplete(w), w), so an unanswered question is a definite NO and this fact resolves FALSE. That is the posture the row calls for and the reason is on the writables: the defect is about WHO may make the return, not about any figure on it, so refusing a population that files correctly today, on screens the application has not built, would trade a paper defect for a real one.
THE THIRD CONDITION IS FOLDED INTO THE FIRST QUESTION, not dropped: section 6013(a)(3) separates "no executor or administrator has been appointed" from "no executor or administrator is appointed before the last day prescribed by law for filing", and the writable asks about both at once ("has been, or will be, appointed"), because at intake time the two are one forward-looking question to the taxpayer.

Fact.Name: The deceased spouse's personal representative is making this joint return
Fact.Description:
SCREEN QUESTION: "Is the personal representative of your spouse's estate (the executor or administrator) making this joint return with you and signing it for your spouse?" Answer YES if you are that personal representative yourself, or if the representative the court appointed will sign this return for your spouse.
HELP TEXT: When a court has appointed, or will appoint, a personal representative for your spouse's estate, the joint return for the year your spouse died is the representative's to make. You can still file it jointly: the representative signs for your spouse, and you sign for yourself. If you are the representative, you sign in both places.
ASKED WHEN: /writableExecutorOrAdministratorAppointedForDeceasedSpouse is answered YES on a return where /inScopeDeceasedSpouse holds. It is asked of no other return.
WHAT THE APPLICATION COLLECTS ALONGSIDE IT, not held in this dictionary: the representative's name, title and signature for the spouse's signature line, or the fact that the surviving spouse is the representative.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: reads as NO. A return with a representative appointed or expected stays refused by /flowKnockoutDeceasedSpouseJointReturnReservedToExecutor exactly as before; only a YES frees it.
VALIDATION: Boolean, a yes/no radio pair.
WHAT IT FEEDS: /deceasedSpouseJointReturnMadeWithoutAuthority and, through it, the knockout.

Fact.Name: This surviving-spouse joint return is being made by someone section 6013(a)(3) does not authorise
Fact.Description:
TRUE when a return for the year has already been made for the decedent, or when a personal representative has been or will be appointed and is NOT the one making this return (/writableDeceasedSpouseJointReturnMadeByPersonalRepresentative not answered YES). This is /deceasedSpouseJointReturnAuthorityDenied narrowed by the representative-signed path: an appointed representative who makes the joint return has the authority the statute gives, and the return files.
THE ALREADY-MADE LEG IS NOT NARROWED. Once a separate return has been made for the decedent, a joint return for that year replaces a separate return, which is a different election with its own time limits and bars; the representative-signed path here does not decide it, so that leg still refuses whoever makes the return.
COMPLETE-SAFE: each writable is read IsComplete-first; with nothing answered this is FALSE, as the fact it narrows is.

Fact.Name: Knockout: this surviving spouse joint return is reserved to the decedent's representative
Fact.Description:
Refuses a married-filing-jointly return on which the spouse died during the tax year, or in the following year before this return is filed (/inScopeDeceasedSpouse), AND the survivor has answered that a personal representative has been or will be appointed and is not the one making this return, or that a return has already been made for the decedent (/deceasedSpouseJointReturnMadeWithoutAuthority). Section 6013(a)(3) gives the joint return to the representative in those cases. A return the representative makes (/writableDeceasedSpouseJointReturnMadeByPersonalRepresentative YES) is not refused: that is the representative-signed path, and the signer's identity is the application's to collect.
WHY A REFUSAL AND NOT A GATE ON /inScopeDeceasedSpouse. That fact is exported to MeF and is what sets the Form 1040 SurvivingSpouseInd; turning it FALSE would strip the indicator and let the same unauthorised joint return file anyway, which is worse than the defect. The return has to stop.
DATA-COMPLETENESS RESIDUE, named because a guard owes one: none. The refusal is not standing in for an unbuilt computation. Every figure on such a return is already correct; what is missing is the authority to make it. The representative-signed path now exists for the appointed-representative leg; the already-made leg still refuses, because a joint return after a separate one is a different election this graph does not decide.

Fact.Name: Knockout: a married-filing-jointly return names a spouse who died before the tax year
Fact.Description: Refuses a married-filing-jointly return when the secondary filer died before the 2025 tax year. The 2025 Form 1040 instructions permit a joint return only when the spouse died during 2025 or during 2026 before the 2025 return is filed; an earlier death is neither permitted timing and this dictionary has no separate-return representative path for that shape.
The age that the spouse may have turned during the year they died

The age at death of the filer when counting the day before their birthday as their birthday. This birthday definition is used for at least the standard deduction and the 25-year minimum age for EITC. It is not used for the 65 year maximum age for EITC.

Fact.Name: Secondary filer age-year difference at death on the actual-birthday convention
Fact.Description: The death year minus the secondary filer's actual birth year. This is the base for the actual-birthday age-at-death test; keep it separate from /secondaryFilerAgeDuringDeathYear, whose year is shifted for the day-before-birthday convention used by the standard deduction and EITC age-25 minimum.

The age of the secondary filer on their date of death, counting their actual date of birth as their birthday. This is used for the 65-year maximum age on self-only EITC, but is not used for the 25-year minimum age, or for standard deduction.

Fact.Name: The primary filer died during the tax year
Fact.Description:
Whether this return reports the death of the taxpayer named FIRST on it, with a date of death to age them by. The spouse-side twin is /isWidowedInTaxYear; this is the primary-filer one, and until this fact existed no age test had a primary-side death branch at all.
THE DATE OF DEATH IS THE ONLY OPERAND. form1040:/writableForm1040PrimaryFilerDeceased is a CONFIRMATION and a routing answer, not a second operand: it opens the printed strip and the signature block, and it supplies no date, so it can refuse or route but it can never relax an age test. Requiring that checkbox as well as the date would make an intake that answers the DATE and leaves the checkbox unanswered read a definite FALSE - and a definite false here routes every age test back to the end-of-year age, so a filer who died on 2025-02-12, two days before reaching 65, would be 65 at year end and would be PAID the Schedule 1-A senior deduction the instructions deny him. A missing checkbox must never buy a deduction, so the date alone is the aging fact, which is also how the spouse-side twin /secondaryFilerDeceasedInTaxYear has always read.
Complete-safe by construction (IsComplete-first), so a return that never saw the question reads a definite FALSE.
THE DEATH MUST FALL IN THE TAX YEAR, which is what the name says and what the last conjunct tests. A taxpayer who dies in 2026 before filing the 2025 return is an ordinary case the Form 1040 instructions contemplate, and that return's taxable year still closed on 2025-12-31: the age tests must read the end-of-year age, not an age at a death that happened after the year ended. The spouse-side twin /isWidowedInTaxYear makes the same comparison on /yearOfSpouseDeath.

Fact.Name: The secondary filer died in the year after the tax year
Fact.Description: Whether the recorded secondary-filer date of death falls in the calendar year after the tax year, which the date's upper bound limits to a death before this return is filed. The spouse was alive at the close of the tax year (IRC 7703(a)(1)), so this is NOT a death in the tax year and feeds no age test; it feeds only /inScopeDeceasedSpouse, the surviving-spouse joint return. Complete-safe: false when the date is unanswered.

Fact.Name: The secondary filer died during the tax year
Fact.Description: Whether the return records a secondary-filer date of death in the current tax year. This is independent of the marital-status answer: a spouse who dies during the tax year is treated as married at the time of death under section 7703(a)(1), so the age-at-death branch must also work when marital status is answered as married. Complete-safe false when the date is unanswered or outside this tax year.

Fact.Name: Primary filer age during the year of death
Fact.Description: The age the primary filer may have turned during the year they died, on the day-before-the-birthday convention: the year of death minus the year of /primaryFiler/dayBeforeDateOfBirth. The exact twin of /secondaryFilerAgeDuringDeathYear, and an intermediate: the two facts below turn it into the two conventions the age tests need. Incomplete unless the date of death is answered; every caller gates on /primaryFilerDeceasedInTaxYear first.

Fact.Name: Primary filer age at death, day before the birthday convention
Fact.Description: The primary filer's age on their date of death, counting the day BEFORE their birthday as their birthday. The exact twin of /secondaryFilerAgeDayBeforeDeath, and the convention the IRS applies to the earned income credit's age-25 minimum and to the age-65 additional standard deduction. It is NOT the convention for the earned income credit's age-65 maximum; /primaryFilerAgeDayOfDeath is.

Fact.Name: Primary filer age-year difference at death on the actual-birthday convention
Fact.Description: The death year minus the primary filer's actual birth year. This is the base for the actual-birthday age-at-death test; keep it separate from /primaryFilerAgeDuringDeathYear, whose year is shifted for the day-before-birthday convention used by the standard deduction and EITC age-25 minimum.

Fact.Name: Primary filer age at death, actual birthday convention
Fact.Description: The primary filer's age on their date of death, counting their actual date of birth as their birthday. The exact twin of /secondaryFilerAgeDayOfDeath. This is the convention for the earned income credit's age-65 MAXIMUM, and it is not the convention for the age-25 minimum or for the standard deduction.

Fact.Name: Whether the deceased spouse turned age 65 in the tax year.
Fact.Description:
The spouse died and turned 65 in the tax year. Calculated using their day of birth as the day before their birthday. Cannot be used for the EIC calculation.
Despite the name, this is no longer only the standard deduction's fact: it is the ONE quantity for "did the deceased spouse reach 65", and the general /filers/*/age65OrOlder reads it directly on its spouse-death arm rather than re-deriving the same comparison. Every age-65 consumer therefore sees a single answer.

Fact.Name: Deceased spouse in the household at death or after June 30
Fact.Description: For a filer whose spouse died during the tax year: whether the spouse was a member of the filer's household at the time of death, or at any time from July 1 through the date of death. For a death before July 1 only the time of death counts. A spouse who was living in the home until the death was a member of the household at the time of death, so the answer is yes; the death itself is not living apart. Temporary absences (illness, business, vacation, military service) do not make the spouse a non-member.

Fact.Description: Whether the filer's spouse died during the tax year, by either intake route: the marital-status answer "widowed" with the year of death in the tax year (/isWidowedInTaxYear), or a secondary-filer date of death in the tax year recorded on a return whose marital status is answered as married (/secondaryFilerDeceasedInTaxYear, complete-safe false when no date is recorded). Used to apply the living-apart test for head of household to a filer whose spouse died in the year.

Whether to ask /writableDeceasedSpouseInHouseholdJulyToDeath: the spouse died during the tax year (/spouseDiedInTaxYear), the filer lived with the spouse six months or less, and the filer answered that they lived apart for the last six months of the year.

It serves the earned income credit's separated-spouse rule only; it does not make the taxpayer unmarried for filing status (a decree of separate maintenance is the legallySeparated marital status).

Fact.Description: Whether the taxpayer was living apart from their spouse and had a written separation agreement or a separate-maintenance decree on the last day of the year; false for a couple who lived together all year. Fact.Name: Qualified to file jointly in year of spouse death
Fact.Description: For the year your spouse died, could a joint return have been filed for the two of you, whether by you or by your spouse's executor or administrator? Answer yes if the only obstacle was who had authority to sign it.

Fact.Name: Marital Status Options
Fact.Description: Options for a marital status. FIVE, not four: section 7703(a)(2) makes an individual legally separated under a decree of divorce or of separate maintenance NOT married for chapter 1 purposes, and until legallySeparated existed such a filer had to answer "married", which forced /eligibleForSingle false and denied them both Single and Head of Household. The option is appended rather than inserted so no existing value's position moves.

Fact.Name: Legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance
Fact.Description:
The filer stated they are legally separated from their spouse under a decree of divorce or of separate maintenance. Section 7703(a)(2) makes such an individual NOT married for chapter 1 purposes, so this status behaves like an unmarried one throughout: /isMarried is false, /maritalStatusAllowsFilingMarried is false and filingStatus:/eligibleForSingle is therefore true, and Head of Household is open on the ordinary qualifying-person test.
NOT THE SAME AS filers:/specialRuleForSeparatedSpouses, and the difference is the point. That fact is the section 7703(b) / section 32(d)(2) machinery for a filer who IS still married and is treated as not married for a particular provision; this one is the section 7703(a)(2) filer who is not married at all. A decree is required either way: a written separation agreement is not a decree and does not reach this status.

Fact.Description: The marital status the primary filer tells us. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (FTB 3514 / FTB 3506 filing-status tests).
