Fact.Name: Check For Registered Domestic Partner
Fact.Description: Whether to show the filer the question to see if they had a registered domestic partner. Only show the question if they chose "never married", "widowed", "divorced or legally separated" and if they RESIDE in a Community Property state OR are DOMICILED in one (Any(RESIDENCE, DOMICILE)). The residence test is deliberately overly broad, avoiding the need to produce an exhaustive list of county and local registries; the domicile arm is there because Publication 555 keys the whole RDP determination on domicile - "Generally, the laws of the state in which the members of the registered domestic partnership are domiciled governs whether the RDP has community income or separate income" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 4, LEFT column of a two column page, the line fragments rejoined) - so an RDP DOMICILED in a community property state but RESIDENT elsewhere still owes an allocation and must still be asked. Over-asking is not a defect, and the answer decides nothing on its own.

Fact.Name: In Registered Domestic Partnership
Fact.Description: Whether the filer was in a registered domestic partnership in the tax year or not.

Fact.Name: Has completed registered domestic partner if applicable
Fact.Description: Checks whether registered domestic partnership is applicable and if so ensures it's complete

Fact.Name: Flow knockout for registered domestic partnership
Fact.Description: Registered domestic partnership is applicable, the filer has one, and neither the filer nor the partner has affirmatively answered a domicile outside every community-property state (Publication 555 keys the RDP community-income determination on domicile, not residence).

The filer is subject to community property laws on THREE arms. ARM 1 is residence: the filer is only eligible for MFS, or chose MFS, or chose HoH and said their marital status is married, and resides in a community-property state (/livesInCommunityPropertyState, the same nine states as the domicile arm below) — UNLESS both the primary and the spouse are affirmatively domiciled outside every community-property state (/bothFilersDomiciledOutsideCommunityPropertyStates), which is the domicile-clears-residence exception: Publication 555 keys the community-or-separate determination on domicile, not residence, so a couple who merely resided in one of these states but are domiciled elsewhere owes no allocation on that residence alone.
ARM 2 is the DOMICILE gate, /isCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn, narrowed by Not(/communityPropertyReturnAllocationInputsComplete): a domiciled return is refused by this arm until the completeness attestation, the IRC 66(a) threshold question and every owed per-item character question are all answered, at which point the eight per-collection allocation facts take over and this arm stops holding it.
ARM 3 is the IRC 66(a) data-completeness arm, /section66aAttestationsUnansweredOnSeparateReturn: a separated spouse whose 66(a) attestations are unanswered stays refused here rather than falling through to an unprotected split.

Fact.Name: The states whose community property laws can reach a separate federal return
Fact.Description:
The option list for /writableDomicileState. NINE community property states plus noneOfThese, tracking constants:/scopedStateOptions by construction rather than by prose: that enum carries every U.S. jurisdiction, so Louisiana is live here together with the matching arm of /livesInCommunityPropertyState. Publication 555's printed list is NINE.
EXPORTED for the same reason hsa:/hsaMonthlyCoverageTypeOptions and form1099Rs:/line4cElectionOptions are: an EnumOptions fact referenced only through an optionsPath contributes no depends_on edge to the facts manifest, so lint_wiring reads it as unconsumed. The repo's two sanctioned answers are an Export or a wiring_skip_list row; the Export is the truthful one here.

Fact.Name: State of domicile
Fact.Description:
The state the primary filer names as their DOMICILE, which is a different question from /filerResidenceAndIncomeState. Domicile is the permanent legal home a person intends to return to; residence is where they lived and earned. Only domicile decides whether income is community income for federal purposes, and this dictionary collected no domicile before this fact existed. UNANSWERED IS THE COMPLETE SAFE STATE: /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState reads false, the allocation gate reads false, and every existing refusal stands unchanged.
NAMED GAP, ONE DOMICILE PER RETURN: this collects the PRIMARY filer's domicile only, and Publication 555 contemplates spouses whose domiciles differ and tells the reader to check the law of each. A separate return whose two spouses are domiciled in different states is therefore not distinguished here from one where both share this answer. The direction is the refusing one wherever the primary is domiciled outside the eight, and the spouse-side intake is the successor unit's to add.

Fact.Name: Domiciled in a community property state
Fact.Description: The DOMICILE twin of /livesInCommunityPropertyState, which tests a RESIDENCE. It names the same NINE states, and it is deliberately a separate fact rather than a rewiring of the residence test: the residence one is read by the shipping knockout and by the flow, and nothing about those changes here. Complete safe by construction, because the IsComplete conjunct is FIRST: an unanswered domicile reads false rather than Incomplete.

Fact.Name: State of spouse's domicile
Fact.Description:
The spouse's state of DOMICILE, the married twin of /writableDomicileState (which collects only the PRIMARY filer's domicile). Publication 555 tells a filer whose spouse has a different domicile to check the law of EACH: "If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 2, RIGHT column of a two column page). Without this answer the dictionary can tell whether the PRIMARY's own income is community property but not whether the SPOUSE's income independently creates a community-property obligation on this return - /writableDomicileState's own Description names this as the gap "the successor unit's to add".
ASKED WHEN: on a return where /isMarried is true and the primary is not filing MFJ (MFS, or married claiming HoH) - the population /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws's residence arm watches. UNANSWERED IS THE COMPLETE SAFE, REFUSING STATE: an unanswered spouse domicile can never CLEAR the community-property refusal - only an affirmatively-answered domicile outside every community-property state, on BOTH sides at once, does - so silence here changes nothing a return can file; it only withholds a possible narrowing. VALIDATION: single-select Enum over /domicileStateOptions, the same nine states plus noneOfThese the primary's own domicile question uses (a person has exactly one domicile). FEEDS: /spouseDomiciledInCommunityPropertyState and, through it, /bothFilersDomiciledOutsideCommunityPropertyStates, the domicile-clears-residence exception on /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws.

Fact.Name: Spouse domiciled in a community property state
Fact.Description: The SPOUSE's twin of /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState, over the same nine states. Complete safe by construction, because the IsComplete conjunct is FIRST: an unanswered spouse domicile reads false rather than Incomplete, so silence cannot make this Incomplete and cannot, on its own, clear anything - the clearing predicate that reads this fact requires BOTH domiciles to be affirmatively answered before it can narrow anything.

Fact.Name: Both the primary filer and the spouse are affirmatively domiciled outside every community property state
Fact.Description:
THE DOMICILE-CLEARS-RESIDENCE PREDICATE the /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws rebody contract's cell (2) named as an open decision. Publication 555 keys the whole community-or-separate determination on DOMICILE, not residence ("The law of the state ... where you are domiciled will determine if you have community property, community income, or both."; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 2, RIGHT column), so a couple both domiciled outside the nine states owes no community-property allocation on their earned income regardless of where either of them physically resided during the year - a population /livesInCommunityPropertyState alone cannot tell apart from a couple actually domiciled inside one - EXCEPT real estate, which Pub. 555's own third community-income bullet characterises by the SITUS of the property rather than either person's domicile (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 3, RIGHT column) and which this predicate does not read.
WHY BOTH DOMICILES, NOT JUST THE PRIMARY'S. Each spouse's OWN income is characterised by THAT spouse's domicile ("Salaries, wages, and other pay received for the services performed by you, your spouse ... while domiciled in a community property state" is community income; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 3, RIGHT column). An MFS return reports the PRIMARY's own income, but half of a community item belongs on the return regardless of WHICH spouse earned it, so a primary domiciled outside every community-property state whose SPOUSE is domiciled inside one still owes an allocation of the spouse's community income. Clearing on the primary's domicile alone would silently file such a return unallocated - a wrong return, not a freed one - which is exactly why /writableDomicileState's own Description names the spouse-side intake as "the successor unit's to add" rather than this predicate being built on the primary alone.
UNANSWERED NEVER CLEARS. Both /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState and /spouseDomiciledInCommunityPropertyState are complete-safe FALSE, so a bare Not() of either would read TRUE on silence and clear an unasked return. This predicate instead requires EACH domicile to be AFFIRMATIVELY ANSWERED (IsComplete on the underlying writable) before it can clear anything; an unanswered domicile on either side leaves this predicate false and the knockout's residence arm refusing exactly as before.

Fact.Name: Domiciled in a state whose community property laws reach a registered domestic partnership
Fact.Description:
The RDP twin of /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState, and it names THREE states rather than nine. Publication 555 is written for RDPs "domiciled in Nevada, Washington, or California" and says those RDPs "must generally follow state community property laws and report half the combined community income". It says nothing about a registered domestic partnership in the other six community property states, and this is the whole reason the two facts are separate rather than one shared test: the MARRIAGE case reaches all nine because a marriage in any of them creates a community, while an RDP's community interest is a creature of the particular state's domestic partnership statute and the only such statutes the vendored text reaches are Nevada's, Washington's and California's.
WHY THIS IS NOT A STATE-BASED REFUSAL, which is the thing the project owner's binding never-refuse-on-state decision forbids. Reading false here REFUSES NOBODY. It is an input to /isRdpCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn only, that gate is read by no shipping guard, and filers:/flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership - which is what actually stops an RDP return - is All(/checkForRegisteredDomesticPartner, /inRegisteredDomesticPartnership) and does not read the gate at all. An Arizona-domiciled RDP is refused after this fact exactly as they were refused before it, on the same guard, for the same reason. What a false reading does is keep this return OUT of an allocation, and that direction is the protective one: once the eight per-collection allocation facts read the gate, a true reading MOVES HALF OF THIS FILER'S WAGES to a partner, and doing that on the strength of a state whose law may grant the partner no community interest at all would be a wrong return with a real dollar figure on it.
Complete safe by construction, because the IsComplete conjunct is FIRST: an unanswered domicile reads false rather than Incomplete.

Fact.Name: State of registered domestic partner's domicile
Fact.Description:
The RDP partner's state of DOMICILE, the RDP twin of /writableSpouseDomicileState (the married twin of /writableDomicileState - this dictionary keeps a separate writable per relationship type rather than reusing one across marriage and RDP, matching the existing /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState / /domiciledInRdpCommunityPropertyState split). Publication 555's "check the laws of each" instruction names the RDP case explicitly: "If you and your spouse (or your RDP) have different domiciles, check the laws of each to see if you have community property, community income, or both." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 2, RIGHT column). Without this answer the dictionary can tell whether the FILER's own income is community property but not whether the PARTNER's income independently creates a community-property obligation on this return.
ASKED WHEN: on a return where /inRegisteredDomesticPartnership is true - the population /flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership watches. UNANSWERED IS THE COMPLETE SAFE, REFUSING STATE: an unanswered partner domicile can never CLEAR the RDP refusal - only an affirmatively-answered domicile outside every community-property state, on BOTH sides at once, does - so silence here changes nothing a return can file; it only withholds a possible narrowing. VALIDATION: single-select Enum over /domicileStateOptions, the same nine states plus noneOfThese the filer's own domicile question uses (a person has exactly one domicile). FEEDS: /partnerDomiciledInCommunityPropertyState and, through it, /bothPartnersDomiciledOutsideCommunityPropertyStates, the domicile-clears-residence exception on /flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership.

Fact.Name: Registered domestic partner domiciled in a community property state
Fact.Description: The PARTNER's twin of /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState, over the same NINE states rather than the RDP-specific three /domiciledInRdpCommunityPropertyState names - clearing a refusal must use the WIDER list (the same asymmetry /domiciledInRdpCommunityPropertyState's own Description explains for the gate: a false reading there is protective because it only withholds an allocation, so the gate can safely use the narrow three; a false reading HERE would CLEAR a refusal, so it must use the wide nine to stay conservative). Complete safe by construction, because the IsComplete conjunct is FIRST: an unanswered partner domicile reads false rather than Incomplete, so silence cannot make this Incomplete and cannot, on its own, clear anything.

Fact.Name: Both the filer and the registered domestic partner are affirmatively domiciled outside every community property state
Fact.Description:
THE RDP TWIN of /bothFilersDomiciledOutsideCommunityPropertyStates, the domicile-clears-residence predicate the /flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership rebody contract's cell (6) named as the identical open decision the community twin's cell (2) names, "taken together or neither." Publication 555 keys the whole RDP community-or-separate determination on DOMICILE, not residence: "Generally, the laws of the state in which the members of the registered domestic partnership are domiciled governs whether the RDP has community income or separate income." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 4, LEFT column). A filer RESIDENT in a community-property state but DOMICILED, along with the partner, entirely outside every one of them owes no allocation on earned income no matter where either of them resided - the ask that shows this question is deliberately over-broad (Any(residence, domicile), by the fact's own Description), but the REFUSAL itself must not be - EXCEPT real estate, which Pub. 555's community-income definition characterises by the SITUS of the property rather than either person's domicile (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 3, RIGHT column, a bullet the same list applies to RDPs as to spouses) and which this predicate does not read.
WHY BOTH DOMICILES, NOT JUST THE FILER'S. Each partner's OWN income is characterised by THAT partner's OWN domicile, the same rule Pub. 555 states for spouses. A filer domiciled outside every community-property state whose PARTNER is domiciled inside one still owes an allocation of the partner's community income once that allocation exists - clearing on the filer's domicile alone would be wrong for the identical reason the community twin's predicate is built on both spouses rather than the primary alone.
UNANSWERED NEVER CLEARS. Both /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState and /partnerDomiciledInCommunityPropertyState are complete-safe FALSE, so a bare Not() of either would read TRUE on silence and clear an unasked return. This predicate instead requires EACH domicile to be AFFIRMATIVELY ANSWERED (IsComplete on the underlying writable) before it can clear anything; an unanswered domicile on either side leaves this predicate false and the knockout refusing exactly as before.
WHY THE NINE-STATE TEST AND NOT THE RDP-SPECIFIC THREE. /domiciledInRdpCommunityPropertyState deliberately reads only nv/wa/ca because a FALSE reading there is protective (it only withholds an allocation the eight per-collection facts would otherwise make). A false reading HERE clears a refusal instead, so the conservative direction reverses: this predicate reads the same NINE-state /domiciledInCommunityPropertyState the community guard uses, on both the filer's and the partner's domicile, so an RDP domiciled in any of the six states Pub. 555 does not name for RDPs specifically (az, id, la, nm, tx, wi) still cannot be cleared by this predicate.

Fact.Name: No joint return was filed with the spouse for the calendar year
Fact.Description: IRC 66(a)(2)(B) as a filer attestation. No printed line of Form 8958 supplies it, so it is a question the application must ask. NOTE THE WINDOW, which is wider than this return: the condition asks about a joint return for a taxable year BEGINNING OR ENDING in the calendar year, so a fiscal year return of either spouse can defeat it. UNANSWERED means the IRC 66(a) exception is NOT ESTABLISHED, and the ordinary community split applies.

Fact.Name: One or both spouses had community EARNED income for the calendar year
Fact.Description: IRC 66(a)(3) as a filer attestation. EARNED income is the statute's own narrower term, defined by cross reference to section 911(d)(2), so interest, dividends and pension income do not answer this question; wages and pay for personal services do. No printed line of Form 8958 supplies it. UNANSWERED means the exception is NOT ESTABLISHED, and the ordinary community split applies.

Fact.Name: No part of that community earned income moved between the spouses
Fact.Description: IRC 66(a)(4) as a filer attestation, and it is the condition most likely to be answered wrongly, so its two exclusions are stated rather than left to the statute's flat words: Publication 555 says a transfer satisfying a CHILD SUPPORT obligation does not count, and neither does a transfer of very small amounts or value. The statute's own words reach transfers made DIRECTLY OR INDIRECTLY and only those made before the close of the calendar year. No printed line of Form 8958 supplies it. UNANSWERED means the exception is NOT ESTABLISHED, and the ordinary community split applies.

Fact.Name: The IRC 66(a) spouses-living-apart rule is established on this return
Fact.Description:
All four conditions of IRC 66(a), each established affirmatively or not established at all. Condition (1), married at any time during the calendar year, is carried by the allocation gate's own marital conjunct rather than repeated here, and the difference is worth naming: IRC 7703(a) fixes marital status as of the CLOSE of the year, while 66(a)(1) asks whether the two were married at ANY time in it, so a couple divorced mid year satisfies the statute and is not reached by this dictionary.
NAMED GAP ON CONDITION (2)(A), and it is the one a reader must not miss. The statute says the spouses must "live apart at all times during the calendar year". What ships is /livedTogetherAllYearWithSpouse, whose FALSE arm covers both "apart at all times" and "together for part of the year" — Publication 555's own "Other separated spouses" paragraph is exactly the second population. So this leg is BROADER than the statute: it can read the rule as established for a couple who separated mid year and whom 66(a) does not reach. The direction of that error is deliberate and it refuses rather than files, because the allocation gate reads this fact NEGATED: a broader 66(a) turns the gate OFF, and an off gate leaves every existing refusal standing. Closing the gap needs an "apart at all times" attestation, which is the successor unit's to add.
Complete safe by construction: every IsComplete conjunct precedes the value it guards, so an unanswered attestation reads false rather than Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Every allocation condition except the IRC 66(a) exception
Fact.Description: The four conjuncts of /isCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn that have nothing to do with IRC 66(a): married, a DECLARED separate return, domiciled in a community property state, and not a registered domestic partnership. Factored out because TWO facts need it — the gate itself, and /section66aAttestationsUnansweredOnSeparateReturn, which must reach exactly the same population before it can refuse one of them. Complete safe by construction: every IsComplete conjunct precedes the value it guards.

Fact.Name: Separated spouses whose IRC 66(a) attestations are unanswered
Fact.Description:
TRUE when this return would otherwise allocate, the spouses did NOT live together all year, and at least one of the three IRC 66(a) attestations has not been answered. It is a DATA COMPLETENESS state, and it exists because the alternative default was the dangerous one.
WHY IT IS NOT ENOUGH TO LET 66(a) READ FALSE ON SILENCE. IRC 66(a) needs all four conditions. /section66aSpousesLivingApartApplies is IsComplete first, so an unanswered attestation makes it FALSE, and a gate that only negates it would then read TRUE and allocate — halving the wages of exactly the separated spouse population 66(a) exists to protect, on the strength of a question nobody answered. Silence is not evidence that the earned income was shared. So the return REFUSES instead: the gate reads false and /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws carries this as one of its arms.
THE ASYMMETRY IS DELIBERATE. An attestation ANSWERED false defeats 66(a) and the ordinary community split applies — that is a filer's answer, and the return computes on it. An attestation UNANSWERED refuses. Answering is what the filer can do; guessing is what this dictionary must not do.
Only the lived apart leg gates it, because a couple who lived together all year is outside 66(a) entirely and is never asked the other three.

Fact.Name: This separate return must allocate community income under Form 8958
Fact.Description:
THE GATE for the whole community property build. True when this return is the separate federal return of a married person domiciled in a community property state, so that half of all community income and all separate income is what belongs on it.
IT USES THE DECLARED STATUS, NOT THE MID INTERVIEW INTENT. The MFS conjunct is filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFS. filingStatus:/treatAsMFS is true for a taxpayer merely ELIGIBLE for MFS who has not declared, and gating an allocation on it would halve the income of someone who goes on to file jointly. A refusal could afford that fact; a computation cannot.
WHY IRC 66(a) TURNS THE GATE OFF RATHER THAN REFINING IT, and what that costs. Where all four conditions are met the statute routes the community income to section 879(a) treatment instead of a split. This gate therefore reads /section66aSpousesLivingApartApplies NEGATED. That is NOT a claim that a 66(a) return allocates nothing: Publication 555's own worked example has the two spouses still reporting "their share of the interest income from community property". The gate goes false because the 879(a) consequence CANNOT BE COMPUTED HERE — section 879 is not vendored in sources/, and this dictionary collects nothing about the community or separate CHARACTER of any single item, which is what 879(a) sorts on. False leaves every existing refusal standing, so the outcome is a data completeness refusal the filer can see, never a wrong return nobody is told about.
AND SILENCE IS NOT AN ANSWER, which is the other half of the same point. /section66aSpousesLivingApartApplies is IsComplete first, so an UNANSWERED attestation makes it false — and a gate that only negated it would then read TRUE and allocate, halving the wages of the separated spouse population on a question nobody answered. So this gate also negates /section66aAttestationsUnansweredOnSeparateReturn: when the spouses did not live together all year and any of the three attestations is unanswered, the gate reads FALSE and the knockout refuses. An attestation ANSWERED false still defeats 66(a) and the ordinary split still applies; only silence refuses.
THE MARRIED HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD ARM IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. filers:/knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws also catches a MARRIED filer claiming head of household. That population needs the IRC 7703(b) abandoned spouse test before anything is allocated to it, which nothing here builds, so the arm is left where it is and the guard keeps refusing it.
THE REGISTERED DOMESTIC PARTNER CONJUNCT IS BELT AND BRACES. An RDP is not married for federal purposes and files single or head of household, so the MFS conjunct already excludes the population. The Not() is stated anyway because this fact CHANGES A NUMBER once its consumers land, and a fact that changes a number states its conditions instead of inheriting them from flow discipline. It is written as "RDP not affirmatively established" rather than as Not(IsComplete(...)), because the RDP question is only asked of unmarried filers and would otherwise be unanswered on every married return.
THIS GATE TESTS DOMICILE, NOT RESIDENCE, WHICH MATTERS FOR WHO /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws CAN CATCH. That guard's residence arm alone (/livesInCommunityPropertyState) does not see a filer DOMICILED in a community-property state but RESIDENT elsewhere, so the guard also fires on THIS GATE directly (Any(residence arm, this gate, the 66(a) data-completeness arm)); without that arm a domiciled-in-CA/resident-in-FL filer would trip no guard at all and would file 100% of wages of which half belong to the spouse. DOLLARS MOVE ON A GATE-TRUE RETURN: each of the eight per-collection allocation facts — formW2s, interest, dividendReports, unemployment, form1099Misc, form1099Rs, each Schedule C business, and the Schedule SE self-employment dotted lines, one per module — reads this gate directly and computes $0 while it is false, so an ordinary return is unaffected. In each allocated collection, the gate being true narrows that collection's own secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ refusal PER ITEM rather than making it disappear: a spouse's document that Form 8958 gives this return half of is lifted and allocated, while a spouse's document that is separate property, or whose community/separate character is unanswered, still refuses — the income aggregate that collection protects is no longer categorically UNSCOPED, but an unresolved item still is. A secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ guard in a collection with no allocation fact of its own (Social Security and HSA distributions, which are disclosed non-allocations, and any collection this build has not yet reached) still refuses categorically, exactly as before. The sharp case, a return carrying only the primary filer's own W-2 with no secondary filer document at all, has no spouse item for any guard to catch and allocates cleanly.
WHAT READS THIS FACT: the eight per-collection allocation facts named above, each its own module.

Fact.Name: (Writable) Every income item of both spouses is entered on this return
Fact.Description:
THE COMPLETENESS ATTESTATION for a community-property allocation return. TRUE means the filer attests that every income item of their own AND every item of their spouse's community income is entered in this return's income collections, so that the Form 8958 halves the per-stream allocation facts compute are halves OF THE WHOLE community income and not of the fragment that happens to be typed in.
WHY IT MUST EXIST, and why the character intakes alone cannot replace it. Form 8958's operative sentence obliges the filer to report half of ALL community income, the spouse's included. The eight allocation streams can halve only what is IN the collections; nothing else in this dictionary can see the spouse's un-entered pension or the W-2 left in a drawer. The sharp case is the gate-true return carrying only the primary filer's own W-2: its wage figure is already the correct half, and what keeps it refusing is exactly that nothing says the spouse had no community income. This attestation is the only thing that can say it.
UNANSWERED IS THE COMPLETE-SAFE STATE AND THE FAIL-CLOSED ONE: /communityPropertyAllocationInputsComplete reads it IsComplete-first, resolves FALSE, and filers:/knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws keeps refusing exactly as it does today. ANSWERED FALSE also keeps refusing: a filer who says the return is missing community income has named the missing-input refusal as their own. Only an affirmative answer can free anything, and only together with every character question answered.
Until an application asks this question, no filer can answer it, so this writable frees nobody.

Fact.Name: Every input the community-property allocation needs is answered
Fact.Description:
TRUE only when a community-property allocation return has everything the eight per-stream allocation facts need to carry the whole Form 8958 split: the completeness attestation /writableAllCommunityIncomeReported answered TRUE, the IRC 66(a) threshold question /livedTogetherAllYearWithSpouse ANSWERED (either way), every present income item's community/separate character answered in all SEVEN characterisable collections (wages, interest, dividends, unemployment, Form 1099-MISC, Form 1099-R, and each Schedule C business), and SELF-EMPLOYMENT INCOME's own two Schedule SE dotted-line entries answered on a return that reports a business. Social security and HSA distributions are disclosed non-allocations, so those two collections owe no character.
SELF-EMPLOYMENT IS THE EIGHTH STREAM AND IT IS GATED ON THE BUSINESS, not demanded of every freed return. Schedule SE's Community Income paragraph applies to "income from a business (including farming)", and a freed community-property MFS return with no Schedule C or F at all -- wages, interest, a Form 8958 with zero self-employment columns -- has nothing to allocate there: its self-employment tax is a Complete $0, not a question left unanswered. So the conjunct is Not(All(business, either dotted-line entry unanswered)) rather than the bare Not(Any(unanswered, unanswered)) the gap was first drafted as; the bare form refused seven committed wage-only fixtures. The FARM leg of the business test is redundant TODAY, because a separate conjunct below already refuses any return claiming a Schedule F, and it is kept deliberately: when the farm allocation lands and that conjunct retires, the self-employment test must keep covering Schedule F without a second edit.
THE livedTogether CONJUNCT IS THE SIXTH-STATE PIN and must not be dropped: with /livedTogetherAllYearWithSpouse unanswered both IRC 66(a) facts read false, the gate reads TRUE, and without this conjunct an attested, fully-characterised return would be freed and would allocate - halving a possibly-separated earner's income on the strength of the one unanswered question that decides whether 66(a) routes it to section 879(a) instead. With it, that return stays refused. COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION, in both engines. Every leg that can be Incomplete is wrapped IsComplete-first, so an unanswered attestation, an unanswered livedTogether, or an ABSENT collection root (Placeholder on the JVM) each makes a conjunct complete-FALSE and this fact resolves FALSE rather than Incomplete. The rollups are read in the NOT direction (characterisationIncomplete false means every owed character is answered), each wrapped in its own IsComplete conjunct.
THE ITEMIZING CONJUNCT IS NOT IN THIS FACT. It is a conjunct of /communityPropertyReturnAllocationInputsComplete, which is All(this fact, the itemizing conjunct) and is what /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws reads. It moved there so it can read the Form 1040 line 12 OUTCOME: this fact is read by Schedule SE, whose inputs reach the standard deduction and the Schedule A total through adjusted gross income, so reading the outcome here would be a dependency cycle. Everything this fact says below about the itemizing conjunct describes that conjunct where it now lives.
THE ITEMIZING CONJUNCT IS NO LONGER A BARE REFUSAL AND IS NOW AN ANSWERABLE QUESTION LIKE EVERY OTHER MEMBER OF ITS All. An itemizing return is freed the moment it attests scheduleA:/writableCommunityPropertyScheduleALine17 - the Schedule A line 17 amount that belongs on THIS separate return after the source-of-funds allocation and the line-specific limits - so the conjunct reads Any(Not(scheduleA:/claimsItemizedDeductions), IsComplete(that writable)).
WHY THE INTAKE IS ENOUGH TO FREE IT, which is the whole of what changed. Form 8958 divides an expense paid from community funds equally and leaves an expense paid from separate funds with the payer (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8958.pdf, page 3, RIGHT column of a two column extraction; Publication 555 lines 442 to 449, LEFT column). The split cannot be computed here because the community-property statutes vary by state and the Schedule A limits are not linear, so the amount is attested rather than derived; the attestation is what the shipping scheduleA:/totalItemizedDeductions already carries to Form 1040 line 12 on an allocation return, and an attested amount that EXCEEDS the unallocated baseline leaves that fact Incomplete, so freeing this gate cannot file an allocation the filer never gave or one larger than the household's own total. Before the intake shipped, freeing such a return would have let the paying spouse deduct 100% of a community expense and lose the other spouse their half - an error in the OPPOSITE direction from the income gaps, so the two did not cancel, which is why the conjunct was a flat refusal until now.
Not(scheduleA:/claimsItemizedDeductions) is still not wrapped in IsComplete because that fact is already complete safe: it reads scheduleA:/hasItemizedDeductions IsComplete first and resolves FALSE when unanswered, so a return that has not been asked about itemizing is not refused by this conjunct and does not need the line-17 answer either.
THE TWO POPULATIONS THIS CONJUNCT USED TO RE-REFUSE WITH NO DEFECT BEHIND THE REFUSAL NOW HAVE A ROUTE OUT. (1) A community-property MFS filer who ANSWERED the itemizing intake TRUE but whose return ultimately takes the STANDARD deduction because it is larger (taxCalculations:/standardOrItemizedDeductions takes the itemized arm only when /wantsStandardDeduction is false) has no itemized deduction on Form 1040 line 12 at all. (2) An MFS filer whose spouse itemizes has a ZERO standard deduction under IRC 63(c)(6)(A) and MUST itemize - scheduleA:/itemizationIsCompulsoryUnderZeroStandardDeduction and filers:/standardDeductionZeroedByMfsSpouseItemizing exist precisely for that population - and used to be knocked out with NO remedy on their part, because itemizing was compulsory and they could not answer their way out the way every other conjunct lets a filer do. Both can now answer line 17 and file.
WHAT IS STILL OWED, and it is a narrower thing than the row that opened this: population (1) is asked for an allocation it does not need, because this conjunct reads the Schedule A INTAKE gate rather than the Form 1040 line-12 OUTCOME. Reading the outcome would take a dependency from this module into taxCalculations, whose own chain runs back through income into filers, so it is a cycle question and not a one-line swap; it stays a named remainder rather than being attempted here.
FIVE CONJUNCTS REFUSE WHAT NOTHING HERE CAN YET ALLOCATE. Form 8958 lines 4, 6 and 8, and the farm half of line 5, have no allocation fact, so a return carrying any of the following would file with the whole amount on the titled or operating spouse: a taxable state or local income tax refund (income:/taxableStateAndLocalIncomeTaxRefunds above $0, Schedule 1 line 1); a Schedule D (scheduleD:/claimsCapitalGainsOrLosses); a capital gain or loss on Form 1040 line 7 by any route (income:/capitalGainsOrLosses not $0, which also catches capital gain distributions reported without a Schedule D); a Schedule F farm (scheduleF:/claimsScheduleFFarmIncome); or any Schedule E activity, tested by presence: a rental, a royalty, a REMIC residual interest or a farm rental claimed (scheduleE:/claimsScheduleERentalIncome, /claimsRoyaltyIncome, /claimsRemicResidualInterest, /claimsFarmRentalIncome), any item of scheduleE:/formK1s or /form1041K1s, or an estate or trust K-1 answered at the return level (scheduleE:/claimsEstateTrustK1), whose income reaches Schedule E line 41 with no /form1041K1s item. Each such return stays refused until its line's allocation is built. A sixth presence conjunct refuses a return that lists any Form 1099-OID (interest:/originalIssueDiscountReports): that form has no community/separate character input and no allocation, so its OID would otherwise stay whole on the filer's return. The refund conjunct reads the TAXABLE refund, the figure the form prints in column A: a refund with no prior-year tax benefit prints $0 and has nothing to allocate. Schedule E is tested by presence rather than by its total because every Schedule E net figure runs through the passive activity loss limitation, whose modified adjusted gross income reaches the Schedule SE community income test, and that test reads this fact; presence refuses more than a nonzero total would, including a Schedule E whose parts net to $0, which still carries items that may be community. Both capital gain conjuncts are kept, because a Schedule D whose gains and losses net to $0 on line 7 still moves each spouse's figure. Every operand is complete safe or read inside IsComplete, so an unrouted refund or an unresolved line 7 leaves its conjunct TRUE: such a return is incomplete on that line itself and files nowhere.
THESE FIVE RE-REFUSE THREE POPULATIONS WITH NO DEFECT BEHIND THE REFUSAL, named so the refusal is not over-read: a state refund that is entirely the filer's separate income; a separately held capital gain or capital gain distribution; a farm that is separate property. Each is released when its line's allocation lands. A Schedule E that is entirely separate property is refused the same way.
WAGES OUTSIDE A FORM W-2 ARE REFUSED UNTIL THEIR SPLIT IS BUILT. Publication 555 treats a spouse's wages as community income that must be evenly split, and Form 1040 line 1 carries four wage streams that no Form W-2 reports: household employee wages (line 1b, income:/unreportedHouseholdWages), tips not reported to the employer (line 1c, Form 4137 line 4), wages of a worker the firm treated as a nonemployee (line 1g, Form 8919 line 6) and H-2A agricultural worker compensation an employer reported in Form 1099-MISC box 3 (line 1h, form1099Misc:/primaryFilerForm1099MiscH2aCompensation and its twin). None of them has a community or separate character or a column B/C split here, so an allocating return that carries any of them above $0 is refused rather than filed with the whole amount on this spouse. Both filers' Form 4137, Form 8919 and H-2A legs are read so the refusal does not depend on which filer slot the separate return's filer occupies. The refusal also covers wages that are this spouse's separate income, which is disclosed: it is released when the streams are characterised.
WAGES OWE A CHARACTER LIKE EVERY OTHER ALLOCATED CLASS. Form 8958 splits wages with no state-law qualifier on its face, but that sentence is about the SPLIT: Publication 555 makes pay community only when earned while domiciled in a community property state and leaves post-separation, pre-decree pay to state law, so a W-2 can be separate property on a return this gate otherwise frees. formW2s:/formW2s/communityPropertyCharacterisationIncomplete is the conjunct that keeps such a return refused until the filer says which.
READ BY exactly one consumer: /communityPropertyReturnAllocationInputsComplete, which is All(this fact, the itemizing conjunct) and is what the allocation-gate arm of /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws narrows the bare gate by (All(gate, Not(that fact))). No SCENARIO answers /writableAllCommunityIncomeReported (the application owes the screens), so this fact is FALSE on every committed scenario; eighteen committed node-test fixtures do answer it TRUE, and they are what pin every conjunct above.

Fact.Name: Every input the community-property allocation needs is answered, including the Schedule A side
Fact.Description:
All(/communityPropertyAllocationInputsComplete, the itemizing conjunct), where the itemizing conjunct is Any(Not(scheduleA:/claimsItemizedDeductions), IsComplete(scheduleA:/writableCommunityPropertyScheduleALine17), standardDeduction:/communityPropertyLine12StandardDeductionWhateverTheAllocation). A community-property separate return that answered the itemizing intake needs the Schedule A line 17 allocation only when itemizing can actually reach Form 1040 line 12: when the household's unallocated itemized total does not exceed the standard deduction and the filer has not elected to itemize, line 12 is the standard deduction whatever the allocation, and the refusal has no defect behind it.
WHY A SEPARATE FACT. /communityPropertyAllocationInputsComplete is also read by Schedule SE (the community-income dotted-line requirement), and the line-12 outcome depends on adjusted gross income, which depends on Schedule SE. Reading the outcome there would close a dependency cycle; reading it here does not, because nothing on the income side reads this fact. /knockoutSubjectToCommunityPropertyLaws reads this fact.
COMPLETE-SAFE: every operand is complete-safe, so this resolves TRUE or FALSE and never Incomplete.

Fact.Name: This return must allocate community income between registered domestic partners
Fact.Description:
THE RDP TWIN of /isCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn. True when this return is the separate federal return of a partner in a registered domestic partnership domiciled in a state whose community property laws reach the partnership, so that half of all community income and all separate income is what belongs on it.
RDP IS NOT A MARRIAGE FOR FEDERAL PURPOSES, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE FACT AND NOT A CASE OF THE MFS ONE. Publication 555: "RDPs aren't married for federal tax purposes. They can use the single filing status or, if they qualify, the head of household filing status." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 2, LEFT column of a two column page, rejoined.) So the filing-status machinery is untouched and ONLY the income-splitting half applies. A fact that treated RDP as "MFS with a different name" would get the filing status wrong on every return it produced.
THE TWO GATES ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE BY CONSTRUCTION, not by convention. This one requires a /maritalStatus in {single, divorced, widowed}; /isCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn requires /maritalStatus = married through /communityPropertyAllocationConditionsBeforeSection66a. One enum, disjoint values, so no return can read both true. Witnessed at both edges: every gate-true fixture below asserts the MFS gate Complete false.
THE MARITAL CONJUNCT IS KEPT HERE RATHER THAN INHERITED FROM THE ASK. /checkForRegisteredDomesticPartner already restricts the RDP question to that same marital set, so on any return the flow actually walks the conjunct is redundant. It is stated anyway because this fact is what the allocation facts will read, and a fact that will change a number states its own conditions instead of borrowing them from a display gate. The DECLARED filing status is used for the same reason - /isFilingStatusSingle or /isFilingStatusHOH, each IsComplete first - rather than the marital-status writable alone.
IT IS A DOMICILE GATE. /filerResidenceAndIncomeState is a RESIDENCE and is deliberately NOT read here. Pub. 555 keys the determination on domicile, and the direction of the error is what settles it: a residence-keyed gate would FREE a Texas-resident, California-domiciled RDP whose income IS community income, and that return would then file unsplit. The input is /domiciledInRdpCommunityPropertyState over the /writableDomicileState intake.
AND IT TESTS PUB. 555'S THREE STATES, NOT THE MARRIAGE CASE'S NINE. /writableDomicileState over /domicileStateOptions is the domicile input this gate reads, so a three-state DOMICILE test is what a domicile gate requires; a three-state RESIDENCE test would be wrong, since keying three states off /filerResidenceAndIncomeState would FREE a Texas-resident, California-domiciled RDP, which is the UNDER-refusing direction.
THE PROJECT OWNER'S NEVER-REFUSE-ON-STATE DECISION IS NOT ENGAGED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE HINGE. Gate-false is not a refusal. This gate is read by no shipping guard; what actually stops an RDP return is /flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership, which is All(/checkForRegisteredDomesticPartner, /inRegisteredDomesticPartnership) and does not read this fact at all. An Arizona-domiciled RDP is refused on that same guard, for the same reason, regardless of this gate. So nothing about the three-state body refuses anyone on the ground of their state, and the never-refuse-on-state decision - which is about REFUSING a federal 1040 - has nothing to bite on.
WHAT THE THREE-STATE BODY DOES DECIDE IS A DOLLAR FIGURE, IN THE PROTECTIVE DIRECTION. Once the eight per-collection allocation facts read this gate, a TRUE reading moves half of this filer's wages to the partner. Pub. 555 says RDPs "domiciled in Nevada," / "Washington, or California. RDPs in Nevada, Washington," / "or California must generally follow state community prop-" / "erty laws and report half the combined community income" (lines 124-125 and 131-134, LEFT column of a two column page). It says NOTHING about a registered domestic partnership in the other six. An RDP's community interest is a creature of the particular state's domestic partnership statute, not of the state's marital community property regime, so a nine-state gate would move half an Arizona-domiciled RDP's wages to a partner whose state law may grant them no community interest at all - a wrong return with a real number on it, arrived at from text that does not say what it was read to say. False on the other six is the reading the vendored text supports, and it is also the one that cannot produce a wrong figure. WHAT READS THIS FACT, AND WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT WIRED. Nothing allocates yet. The eight per-collection allocation facts (formW2s:/communityPropertyAllocatedWages and its seven siblings) each consume the MFS gate alone; folding this population in would make the condition each of them wants Any(/isCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn, /isRdpCommunityPropertyAllocationReturn), not a second copy of the allocation arithmetic. That wiring belongs with those facts and is not done here, to avoid two units of work editing one fact at once.
NOT ONE DOLLAR MOVES, AND THE REFUSAL STAYS UP. /flowKnockoutHasApplicableRegisteredDomesticPartnership keeps shipping and keeps refusing every return this gate reads true, because knowing that a return must allocate is not the same as being able to allocate it: every income aggregate is unscoped, and an RDP's partner is not on this return at all, so there is no intake anywhere for the partner's half.
TWO FEDERAL CONSEQUENCES OF RDP STATUS ARE NAMED AND NOT BUILT, because both condition on an allocation that does not exist yet. (1) THE EARNED-INCOME BAR: a partner "cannot use the other partner's earnings in computing his or her earned income" for the dependent care credit, the refundable portion of the child tax credit, or the earned income credit (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 4, RIGHT column, rejoined). Nothing puts a partner's earnings into any earned-income figure yet, so there is nothing yet for the bar to remove; it becomes owed by whichever fact first allocates earned income into this return. (2) THE STANDARD DEDUCTION IS INDEPENDENT: an RDP "may itemize or claim the standard deduction regardless of whether his or her partner itemizes" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 4, RIGHT column, rejoined), the exact opposite of IRC 63(c)(6)(A). /standardDeductionZeroedByMfsSpouseItemizing is reached only through the MFS filing status, which this population never has, so the two do not share a gate and must not be made to.
THE PARTNER DOMICILE IS NOT A SECOND QUESTION HERE, and this fact decides that rather than leaving it open. /writableDomicileState is the PRIMARY filer's domicile, and Pub. 555 says that where the two partners' domiciles differ the reader must "check the laws of each" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, page 2, RIGHT column, rejoined). That is an instruction to consult state law, not a rule this dictionary could apply: no vendored text says what a federal return does when the domiciles differ. Collecting a partner domicile we have no rule for would add a question whose answer changes nothing, so the gate reads the primary filer's domicile alone and the differing-domicile case is a named gap on the contract record, not a silent one.
