Fact.Description: Neither filer could be claimed as a dependent.

Fact.Name: Year of Spouse Death Options
Fact.Description: The year that a taxpayer's spouse died

Fact.Name: Year of spouse's death
Fact.Description: The relative year a widowed filer's spouse died.

Fact.Name: The spouse's death was determined while the spouse was in missing status from combat zone service
Fact.Description:
SCREEN QUESTION: "Was your spouse listed as missing (missing in action or missing status) because of service in a combat zone, and was your spouse's death determined by the military or the federal employer while your spouse was still listed as missing?"
HELP TEXT: This applies to a member of the uniformed services or a federal civilian employee whose missing status was officially recorded, and whose death was later officially determined. If your spouse's death was not handled this way, answer No.
ASKED WHEN: the filer's marital status is widowed and the year of the spouse's death (/yearOfSpouseDeath) is the tax year or one of the two years before it. For a death dated in one of the two earlier years the answer can close the qualifying surviving spouse status; for a death determined in the tax year it can open it. It is asked of no other return.
WHY IT IS ASKED. For the qualifying surviving spouse test only, a spouse who died in combat-zone missing status is treated as dying on the EARLIER of the date the death was determined and the date two years after the designated end of combatant activities in that zone. The year the filer entered is the determination year; the second date can be earlier and close the qualifying surviving spouse window sooner.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: reads as No and changes nothing, so a return that never sees this screen resolves exactly as before the question existed.
VALIDATION: Boolean, a yes/no radio pair.
WHAT IT FEEDS: /spouseMissingStatusDeemedDeathBeforeQssWindow, and through it /widowedCouldQualifyForQSS.

Fact.Name: The date designated as the termination of combatant activities in the spouse's combat zone
Fact.Description:
SCREEN QUESTION: "What date was designated as the end of combatant activities in the combat zone where your spouse served?"
HELP TEXT: Combat zones are designated, and their end dates set, by Executive order. Leave this blank if no end date has been designated for that zone. Also leave it blank if the zone is the one designated for the Vietnam conflict, because the two-year rule does not apply to that zone.
ASKED WHEN: /writableSpouseDeathDeterminedWhileInCombatZoneMissingStatus is answered Yes.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: no second date, so the determination year the filer already gave governs, exactly as before this question existed. An answered date only ever moves the deemed death EARLIER (the statute takes the earlier date), so it can close the qualifying surviving spouse window sooner and never opens it.
VALIDATION: a calendar date. Only its year is read.
WHAT IT FEEDS: /spouseMissingStatusDeemedDeathBeforeQssWindow.

Fact.Name: The combat-zone missing-status rule puts the spouse's deemed death before the qualifying surviving spouse window
Fact.Description:
TRUE when the spouse's death was determined while in combat-zone missing status and two years after the answered termination date falls in a calendar year EARLIER than the second year before the tax year: termination year plus 4 is less than the tax year. Section 2(a)(3) takes the earlier of the determination and that date, so the deemed death is then no later than that year, outside "either of his two taxable years immediately preceding the taxable year", and the filer is not a surviving spouse whatever year the determination fell in.
YEAR ARITHMETIC IS EXACT HERE. Two years after a date falls in the calendar year two later, so the test needs only the termination year and constants /taxYear; it is not a tax-year constant.
THIS IS THE CLOSING ARM. Its twin, /spouseMissingStatusDeemedDeathInQssWindow, is the opening arm: a determination made in the tax year itself with the two-years-after date inside the window moves the deemed death back into the window.
COMPLETE-SAFE: each input is read IsComplete-first; an unanswered question resolves FALSE and changes nothing.

Fact.Name: The combat-zone missing-status rule puts a death determined in the tax year inside the qualifying surviving spouse window
Fact.Description:
TRUE when the spouse's death was determined during the tax year itself (/yearOfSpouseDeath is taxYear), the death was determined while the spouse was in combat-zone missing status, and two years after the answered termination date falls in one of the two calendar years before the tax year (termination year plus 2 is the tax year minus 1 or minus 2). Section 2(a)(3) treats the death, for the surviving spouse test only, as occurring on the EARLIER of the determination and that date, so the deemed death falls in "either of his two taxable years immediately preceding the taxable year" and the filer can be a surviving spouse for the tax year although the determination was made during it.
WHY IT IS BUILT. The statute states the date rule without exception for this order of dates. The joint return the filer may also make for the year of the determination is a different return (it carries the spouse's items and needs the representative's authority), so it does not stand in for the surviving spouse status the statute grants.
YEAR ARITHMETIC IS EXACT HERE, as for the closing arm: two years after a date falls in the calendar year two later.
COMPLETE-SAFE: each input is read IsComplete-first; an unanswered question resolves FALSE and changes nothing.

Fact.Name: (Writable) Bona fide residence in a U.S. possession for the tax year
Fact.Description:
THE SEPARATING QUESTION for /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState. Before it, the single answer /filerResidenceAndIncomeState == noneOfThese covered TWO POPULATIONS WITH OPPOSITE CORRECT ANSWERS and the dictionary could tell them apart with neither a fact nor a question: a U.S. citizen living abroad or using an APO/FPO address, who files an ordinary Form 1040 and was being refused WRONGLY, and a bona fide resident of a U.S. possession, who does not file a plain 1040 at all. This is that question, asked PER FILER because the residual it splits exists on both sides of an MFJ return.
===== SCREEN SPECIFICATION (operator rule: the application builds the screen from this Description and never re-opens an IRS document) =====
QUESTION TEXT, as it should be asked, for the primary filer: "Were you a bona fide resident of American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands for the 2025 tax year?" And for the spouse, on an MFJ return, the same question in the third-person spouse form the rest of the spouse screens use: "Was [spouse first name] a bona fide resident of American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands for the 2025 tax year?" THE WORDING "FOR THE 2025 TAX YEAR" IS LOAD BEARING. Do not ask "for all of 2025", which contradicts this screen's own help text and manufactures a wrong No: the presence test is 183 days (26 U.S.C. 937, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section937&num=0&edition=2024), not the whole calendar year, and Publication 570 chapter 1 carries an "Exception for Year of Move" - "If you are moving to or from a territory during the year, you may still be able to meet the closer connection test for that year" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 9, RIGHT column). A filer present 200 days, or one who moved mid year, IS a bona fide resident and would answer "for all of 2025" No. The publication's own phrasing is "for the tax year" (lines 328-330, RIGHT column) and that is what the screen asks. NAME ALL FIVE TERRITORIES IN THE QUESTION ITSELF. Do not shorten it to "a U.S. territory" or "a U.S. possession": those phrases are not what a filer calls the place they live, and the wrong answer here is the one that decides whether a whole return is filed.
HELP TEXT, paraphrasing Publication 570 chapter 1 (Bona Fide Residence) in the filer's own language, cite https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 4, RIGHT column of a two column extraction: "Living in one of these territories is not by itself enough. Generally you were a bona fide resident of a territory for the 2025 tax year if ALL THREE of these were true for that territory: - you met the presence test (generally you were there at least 183 days during 2025); - your tax home was not outside the territory; and - you did not have a closer connection to the United States, or to a foreign country, than to the territory. If you moved to or from a territory during 2025 you may still meet the closer connection test for that year. Answer No if you were a U.S. citizen simply living or working abroad. Living abroad does not change how you file a federal return. If you are a member of the Armed Forces who was a bona fide resident of one of these territories in an earlier year and were away from it during 2025 in compliance with military orders, answer Yes. Being in a territory solely in compliance with military orders does not by itself make you a bona fide resident." THE ANSWER INSTRUCTION MUST NOT MENTION AN APO OR FPO ADDRESS. An APO/FPO address is a reason this question gets ASKED - it is one of the mailing addresses that leave a filer with no U.S. jurisdiction to name - and it is NOT a reason to answer No. Publication 570 chapter 1's "Special rule for members of the U.S. Armed Forces" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 4, RIGHT column, continuing at lines 347-357, LEFT column across the page break) says an earlier-year bona fide resident whose "absence from that territory during the current tax year in compliance with military orders will not affect your status as a bona fide resident", and that filer very plausibly has an APO or FPO address. Telling them to answer No is the wrong-return direction. The same span's second half - "being in a territory solely in compliance with military orders will not qualify you for bona fide residency" - is carried too, because it is the other half of the same rule. SECOND HELP PARAGRAPH, the consequence, so the filer understands why the answer matters, cite https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 3, LEFT column (the same proposition is at lines 131-133, RIGHT column): "Bona fide residents of the CNMI, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands generally do not have a U.S. federal income tax return filing obligation at all, and bona fide residents of Puerto Rico and American Samoa exclude their territory source income from a U.S. return. If you answer Yes we will stop and tell you this tool cannot prepare your return, because filing you on a plain Form 1040 would overstate your income."
ASKED WHEN. Ask the primary filer's copy whenever /filerResidenceAndIncomeState == noneOfThese, i.e. immediately after the residence screen when the filer says no U.S. state or district applies. Ask the SPOUSE's copy on the same screen, on an MFJ return, whenever the primary's copy is asked - and only then. Asking either copy anywhere else is harmless but pointless: the guard reads both answers ONLY on a noneOfThese return, so an answer collected elsewhere changes nothing.
NAMED GAP, AND IT IS THE HALF OF THE SPOUSE SIDE NOTHING HERE REACHES. An MFJ return whose PRIMARY names a U.S. state and whose SPOUSE is a bona fide possession resident is not asked this question and is not refused by this guard. That is deliberate: /spouseLivesInTPState is a three member enum (sameState, moreThanOne, noneOfTheAbove) with no jurisdiction keys, so there is no answer on that screen that means "my spouse lives in a possession" rather than "my spouse lives in another state", and gating this question on noneOfTheAbove would put it to the large, correct, federally uninteresting different-state population. Closing that half needs the spouse residence screen to name jurisdictions; naming it here is the /writableDomicileState precedent of "NAMED GAP, ONE DOMICILE PER RETURN" in this file. THAT SCOPING IS NOT A SHORTCUT. A bona fide resident of a possession who has income from outside it files a U.S. return as well as a territory one (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 21, LEFT column), and this dictionary already serves that filer deliberately: eleven committed ctcOdc fixtures pin a bona fide Puerto Rico resident who answers a NAMED state and reaches Schedule 8812 Part II-B, one of them pinning /flowIsKnockedOut Placeholder false. A Yes here must therefore NOT refuse a named-state return; it is read only where the residence answer has already left the dictionary unable to tell the two populations apart.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: REFUSED, deliberately, and this is the load bearing half of the design. An unanswered copy leaves /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState exactly where it stands for a noneOfThese filer: refusing. The alternative posture, defaulting to No, would SILENTLY RELEASE the possession resident onto a plain Form 1040 that overstates gross income, which is the wrong-return direction rather than the refused-access direction. THE SAME POSTURE APPLIES TO THE SPOUSE'S COPY on an MFJ return, and to a return on which the graph cannot yet tell whether there IS a spouse: an unanswered spouse copy must never be treated as cleared. Every committed fixture and scenario in this repo leaves this writable unanswered - measured by parsing every JSON under the repository's tests and scenarios (4,181 files, 3,488 answers of /filerResidenceAndIncomeState) for the ANSWERED value rather than by grepping for the option name: EXACTLY ONE committed artifact answers noneOfThese and it still refuses.
VALIDATION. Boolean, rendered as a required Yes/No pair. There are no other options: a filer who is unsure should be shown the three part test again rather than offered a "not sure" answer, because there is no third posture in the graph for it. No Min, no Max.
WHAT IT FEEDS. /filers/*/isBonaFidePossessionResident (the complete safe alias below), from there /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident and /secondaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident, and from there /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState, which is a flow:/flowIsKnockedOut member. It feeds NO dollar line and no printed field. On a noneOfThese return NOTHING RELEASES UNTIL EVERY FILER THE SCREEN ASKS HAS ANSWERED No: the primary's No is necessary, and on an MFJ return the spouse's No is necessary too. A Yes from either filer holds the return refused, and so does silence from either filer: a spouse copy that is merely unanswered must never release an MFJ return.
===== RELATION TO THE PUERTO RICO ATTESTATION THAT ALREADY SHIPS, stated because "one quantity, one fact" is a rule of this repo and this is the fact nearest to breaking it. ctcOdc:/writableIsBonaFidePuertoRicoResident (dictionary/ty2025/ctcOdc.xml, the Schedule 8812 Part II-B routing input) asks the same TEST of the same filer about ONE of the five territories, and only about Puerto Rico. This fact is the SUPERSET quantity: five territories, per filer, and asked of a population Schedule 8812 never reaches. They are not the same quantity and neither derives the other, so neither is a re-derivation of the other. BUT THEY MUST NOT CONTRADICT EACH OTHER: a return on which ctcOdc:/isBonaFidePuertoRicoResident is true and this attestation is answered No is incoherent, and the consistency wire lives on the downstream fact, not on this writable or its alias: /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident reads Not(ctcOdc:/isBonaFidePuertoRicoResident) as its own conjunct, so a primary filer who answered No here but whose Schedule 8812 intake separately attests a bona fide Puerto Rico residence is no longer treated as CLEARED, and /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState keeps refusing them. It is a one-directional implication (PR resident true defeats this clearance), never the reverse, because the other four territories have no ctcOdc question at all, and the wire does not SET this fact or its alias to any value - see /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident's own Description for why adopting ctcOdc's value as truth would itself be wrong. On a noneOfThese return, a bona fide resident of GUAM who answers Yes here is refused by /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState directly, needing no ctcOdc involvement at all; on a return that names a state, that same Guam resident is NOT refused (this fact reads only inside the noneOfThese gate), which is exactly why the reverse wire - making ctcOdc's PR attestation true from this fact - would be TAX-WRONG rather than merely unnecessary: it would turn that unrefused, named-state Guam resident into a bona fide Puerto Rico resident inside ctcOdc, routed into Schedule 8812 Part II-B and the section 933 line 2a treatment. That formula is WITHDRAWN. The wire is currently one-sided by construction on the SECONDARY filer as well: /secondaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident carries no ctcOdc conjunct of its own, since Schedule 8812's Puerto Rico attestation has no per-filer index to read.
===== WHY A BOOLEAN AND NOT A FIVE MEMBER ENUM. Nothing this unit builds needs to know WHICH territory: the answer Yes refuses whatever the territory is, and the reasons differ by territory only in the residue prose below, not in the graph. An enum member "puertoRico" would also re-collect, in a second place, the datum ctcOdc already collects. If the Yes arm is ever released territory by territory, the successor shape is this Boolean plus a territory Enum asked only behind a Yes, not a replacement of this fact.

Fact.Name: Filer is a bona fide resident of a U.S. possession
Fact.Description:
THE COMPLETE SAFE ALIAS half of the trio idiom, alongside the writable above. Resolves the filer's attestation when it is answered and FALSE when it is not, so that no consumer of it can be dragged Incomplete by an unasked question. The shape is copied term for term from ctcOdc:/isBonaFidePuertoRicoResident, and the predicate in front of the answer is IsComplete on the BARE WRITABLE, which is a real "was the source answered" test rather than IsComplete on a complete safe fact (which would be true on every return and would silence the writable entirely).
THE FALSE ARM IS NOT THE SAFE ANSWER AND THE SAFETY DOES NOT COME FROM IT. Read alone, a FALSE here says "not a possession resident", which is the answer that RELEASES a return. What keeps an unanswered return refused is /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident below, which requires the answer to have been GIVEN before it will release anything; this fact is only the value half. Any future consumer that reads this path directly and treats false as "asked and answered no" is wrong; read /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident instead.
CONSUMERS: /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident and /secondaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident, both below, and through them /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState.

Fact.Name: The primary filer was ASKED the possession residence question and answered No, and that answer is not contradicted by the Puerto Rico attestation Schedule 8812 already collects
Fact.Description:
TRUE only when the primary filer's /writableIsBonaFidePossessionResident is ANSWERED and answered NO. False when it is unanswered, and false when it is answered Yes. This is the "source answered" predicate the narrowing of /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState turns on, and it is a separate fact from the value alias on purpose: the guard must distinguish "said no" from "said nothing", and a Boolean alias that reads false in both cases cannot.
COMPLETE SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION. IsComplete always resolves, and /primaryFiler/isBonaFidePossessionResident is complete safe, so this fact never introduces an Incomplete of its own. It does inherit the Incompleteness of /primaryFiler itself, which is a Find over /filers; every return has a primary filer, and a return that does not is already Incomplete everywhere.
THE THIRD TERM IS THE CONSISTENCY WIRE this fact carries: Not(ctcOdc:/isBonaFidePuertoRicoResident). A primary filer who answered No here but whose Schedule 8812 intake separately attests a bona fide Puerto Rico residence (ctcOdc:/writableIsBonaFidePuertoRicoResident true) gave two contradictory answers to the SAME statutory test (IRC 937(a)) about the SAME territory, and this fact must not read that as "cleared" merely because the residence screen said No. ONE-DIRECTIONAL AND NEVER THE REVERSE: ctcOdc's attestation covers Puerto Rico only, one of the five territories this writable's Yes/No covers, so a False here (this writable unanswered, or answered Yes, or ctcOdc silent) never sets ctcOdc's attestation to anything — nothing on the ctcOdc side reads this path. The two facts remain, as the writable's own Description states, NOT a re-derivation of one another: they are different quantities (five territories here, Puerto Rico only there) that must merely not contradict. WHY THIS TERM AND NOT A CHANGE TO /filers/*/isBonaFidePossessionResident (THE GENERIC ALIAS, REJECTED). The alias is defined once for the whole /filers/* collection and applies to every filer in it, primary and secondary alike; ctcOdc's attestation is a single return-level fact with no filer index, so wiring it into the generic alias would ALSO force the SECONDARY filer's copy true whenever the PRIMARY (or either spouse — the Schedule 8812 "you" does not distinguish) attested Puerto Rico residence to ctcOdc, incorrectly attributing Puerto Rico residence to a spouse who was never asked and may in fact live in Guam or nowhere unusual at all. Gating this specific primary-only "attested and cleared" predicate instead has the narrower, correct blast radius: it holds the PRIMARY's own clearance hostage to the PRIMARY-facing contradiction and touches nothing about the secondary filer's own answer. WHY REFUSE RATHER THAN ADOPT ctcOdc's VALUE AS TRUTH. This fact does not set /primaryFiler/isBonaFidePossessionResident to true when ctcOdc is true — doing so would assert, as fact, that the No answered on THIS screen was wrong, which this dictionary cannot know (it could equally be the ctcOdc attestation that is wrong, e.g. answered by mistake on a screen the filer clicked through). Instead this predicate simply stops treating the primary as CLEARED, which is the same "unanswered-intake residue, correct permanent refusal" idiom this file already uses for every other data-completeness contradiction — see WHAT STILL REFUSES on /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState below. The return stays refused until the contradiction is resolved by whichever screen is wrong changing its answer, not until this dictionary guesses which one that is. THE FORMULA CONSIDERED AND WITHDRAWN, NAMED SO IT IS NOT REPROPOSED: `ctcOdc:/isBonaFidePuertoRicoResident := Any(today's own body, filers:/primaryFiler/isBonaFidePossessionResident)` — writing INTO ctcOdc from filers. That implements the OPPOSITE implication (possession-true ⇒ PR-true) and is tax-wrong: a bona fide resident of Guam answers Yes to the five-territory question, names a state, is not refused by this guard, and would have been turned into a bona fide Puerto Rico resident inside ctcOdc, routed into Schedule 8812 Part II-B and the section 933 line 2a treatment. That formula is WITHDRAWN and nothing here reintroduces it; the wire below reads OUT of ctcOdc into filers, never the reverse, and never through the ctcOdc fact itself.

Fact.Name: The secondary filer position is cleared: there is no spouse, or the spouse was ASKED the possession residence question and answered No
Fact.Description:
A per-filer Boolean whose own asked-when puts the spouse's copy on the same screen as the primary's whenever the primary's is asked. It is the mirror of /primaryFilerAttestedNotAPossessionResident above: it is TRUE only when the spouse side has been CLEARED, and the guard refuses until it is - an AFFIRMATIVE spouse answer is not the only thing that must refuse: a spouse copy that was never answered must refuse too, or an MFJ return whose primary answered No and whose spouse copy was never answered would file an ordinary Form 1040 for a bona fide possession resident, which is exactly the wrong-return direction this fact exists to prevent.
WHY THIS DOES NOT NEED THE /spouseLivesInTPState ASYMMETRY. /spouseLivesInTPState is a THREE MEMBER RESIDENCE ENUM WITH NO JURISDICTION KEYS, where refusing on noneOfTheAbove would sweep in every different-state spouse; that reasoning is about a DIFFERENT FACT and does not transfer here. There is no large correct population to protect: the only returns that reach this fact inside the guard are MFJ returns already inside the noneOfThese gate, and what is left when the spouse has not answered is the ordinary unanswered-intake residue, which is the correct permanent refusal. The gap that /spouseLivesInTPState genuinely cannot close is a different one and is still named on /filers/*/writableIsBonaFidePossessionResident above: an MFJ return whose PRIMARY names a U.S. state and whose spouse is a possession resident is never asked at all.
THE THREE ARMS, AND THE THIRD ONE IS THE ONE THAT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. (a) A return that is KNOWN not to be MFJ resolves TRUE - there is no spouse to ask, so the spouse side is cleared and the guard's disjunct (2) contributes nothing. /secondaryFiler is a Find over /filers and is Incomplete on every single, HOH and QSS return, so this arm is also what keeps the knockout out of the non-MFJ corpus: a Switch never evaluates the branch it does not take. (b) A return that is KNOWN to be MFJ and HAS a second filer asks the same two-part question the primary limb asks: was the spouse's copy ANSWERED, and was the answer No. (c) ANYTHING ELSE resolves FALSE, i.e. NOT CLEARED, i.e. the guard keeps refusing. That covers a return whose filing status has not been answered yet and whose /wantsJointReturn has not been answered either, and an MFJ return whose second filer does not exist yet. THIS ARM IS EASY TO GET WRONG BY WRAPPING TOO LITTLE. filingStatus:/treatAsMFJ IS NOT COMPLETE-SAFE: with /filingStatus unanswered it evaluates Any(false, All(true, /wantsJointReturn, /eligibleForMFJ)), which is Incomplete while /wantsJointReturn is unanswered, and a Switch whose When is Incomplete drags its consumer Incomplete - which on a flow knockout reads as Placeholder false, i.e. AS A RELEASE. Wrapping the When in IsComplete(treatAsMFJ) alone is NOT enough: that alone routes the mid-interview MFJ return to a FALSE spouse limb, which is the same silently-releases-an-unanswered-spouse defect this fact exists to close. The IsComplete test is kept, and the arm behind it is TRUE-refuses rather than FALSE-releases. IsComplete ON A DERIVED FACT IS DELIBERATE HERE and does not break the usual rule against IsComplete over a complete-safe fact: filingStatus:/treatAsMFJ is demonstrably NOT complete-safe (the measurement is in the paragraph above), so this is a real "is the source answered" test, not a tautology. The IsComplete over /secondaryFiler itself is the shipping idiom at form8919.xml:563-565.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION. Every Case's When is an All whose first term is an IsComplete, so no When can be Incomplete; every Then is either a literal or an All over an IsComplete and a Not of a complete-safe alias. AND IT IS READ ONLY INSIDE THE noneOfThese GATE. /flowKnockoutUnsupportedState wraps both its disjuncts in the residence equality, so an uncleared spouse side on a return that NAMES a state refuses nothing. That is deliberate: a bona fide possession resident with income from outside the possession files a U.S. return alongside the territory one (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 21, LEFT column), and eleven committed ctcOdc fixtures already serve exactly that filer on a named-state return.

Fact.Name: No U.S. jurisdiction to name, and not yet separated from a bona fide possession residence
Fact.Description:
State of residence is never a ground for refusing a federal 1040 (project invariant #7 as amended), and constants:/scopedStateOptions carries every U.S. jurisdiction the Form 1040 instructions name, so this guard does not fire on any named state or on the moreThanOne answer.
THE OUTER GATE keys on the single answer /filerResidenceAndIncomeState == noneOfThese. THE PRECISE RELATION TO THE PRINTED PAGE: the instructions' fifth "Where Do You File?" row reads "A foreign country, U.S. territory*, or use an APO or FPO" / "address, or file Form 2555 or 4563, or are a dual-status" / "alien" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 126), and that row is a MAILING-ADDRESS routing rule, not an enum. It is BROADER than this answer in one direction - a Form 2555 filer resident in California is in the row and answers 'ca' here, and is carried by form2555:/knockoutFilesForm2555 and by the citizen/resident-alien gate, not by this fact. What noneOfThese does name is every filer with no U.S. jurisdiction to give, and inside it sits the population the row's footnote sends to Pub. 570: a bona fide resident of a U.S. possession, who does not file a plain 1040 (IRC 933 for Puerto Rico, IRC 931 for American Samoa / Guam / the CNMI, with Form 4563 and Form 8689 carrying them).
/hasIncomeInScope's own body is untouched by this guard: filers:/filingStateOrProvince still reads it, and it is the honest record of what the intake answers imply about state filing even though nothing here refuses on them.
/filers/*/writableIsBonaFidePossessionResident is the intake that separates that filer from a citizen abroad who WOULD file an ordinary 1040, and this body reads it through two disjuncts inside the outer gate: (1) the primary filer has NOT answered the possession residence question with a No; and (2) the SECONDARY filer position has NOT been CLEARED. On an MFJ return the spouse's copy must have been ANSWERED No; a spouse Yes refuses, an unanswered spouse copy refuses, and a return whose filing status is not yet answered refuses. On a return known not to be MFJ this disjunct contributes nothing. SILENCE ON EITHER SIDE IS NEVER A NO: an MFJ return whose primary answered No and whose spouse copy was never answered must stay refused, not file. Negative control on the outer gate.
WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: a third, UNGATED disjunct refusing any return whose primary attested Yes on ANY residence answer. That would WIDEN this guard past the outer gate. A bona fide resident of a possession who has income from outside it files a U.S. return alongside the territory one (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 21, LEFT column of a two column extraction), and this dictionary already serves that filer on purpose: eleven committed ctcOdc fixtures pin a bona fide Puerto Rico resident answering a NAMED state. WHAT DOES NOT REFUSE. A U.S. citizen living abroad, or using an APO or FPO address, who has no U.S. jurisdiction to name and every one of whose filers answers No to the possession residence question, files an ordinary Form 1040. Every one of those six paths carries Export mef="true" - verified by reading the Export element of each fact, /wages at formW2s.xml:10725 and the other five in taxCalculations.xml - so every dollar this releases reaches a printed and transmitted line rather than an internal subtotal. Also pinned for a single filer with no spouse at all, which exists to prove that disjunct (2) does not drag this guard Incomplete on a return that has no secondary filer.
WHAT STILL REFUSES. Two things, and neither is a state. (i) THE UNASKED noneOfThese FILER, ON EITHER SIDE OF THE RETURN, AND A RETURN WHOSE FILING STATUS IS NOT YET ANSWERED. Silence is not a No. An unanswered attestation - the primary's copy, the spouse's copy on an MFJ return, or a return on which the graph cannot yet tell whether there IS a spouse - leaves this guard refusing, which is the whole reason the writable's unanswered posture is REFUSED: defaulting it to No would silently release a bona fide possession resident onto a plain Form 1040 that overstates gross income, which is the wrong-return direction. This limb retires when the application ships the screen. (ii) THE noneOfThese FILER WHO ANSWERS YES, and on an MFJ return the one whose SPOUSE does. This is the honest permanent residue - a filer with no U.S. jurisdiction to name who IS a bona fide possession resident - and it is stated per territory rather than as one sentence, because the reasons differ: - CNMI, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands: a bona fide resident "generally does not have a U.S. federal income tax return filing obligation" at all (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p570.pdf, page 3, LEFT column of a two column extraction; the same proposition, more cleanly set, at lines 131-133, RIGHT column: "Because bona fide residents of the CNMI, Guam, and" / "the U.S. Virgin Islands generally do not have a federal in-" / "come tax return filing obligation"). The right answer is not a differently computed 1040; it is not filing one, and Form 8689 is filed by a NON bona fide resident with USVI source income, so it does not serve this population either. - Puerto Rico and American Samoa: the IRC 933 and IRC 931 exclusion arithmetic DOES ship (ctcOdc:/puertoRicoIncomeExclusion933, ctcOdc:/possessionIncomeExclusion931 over the Form 4563 Part II component lines) and so does the Pub. 570 chapter 4 apportionment (income:/grossIncomeSubjectToUsTax), so ctcOdc does not stand in front of this population as a class: ctcOdc:/knockoutPossessionOrPuertoRicoIncomeExclusion is a data-completeness refusal, not a scope refusal, and does not fire on a possession filer who enters $0 or who answers its companion intakes. What still makes a Yes unsafe here is that fact's own named residual - a return it releases can still compute WRONG in ways nothing downstream can see - and that residual, not this guard, is why the Yes arm stays refused.

Fact.Name: Care expenses in this amount that were paid to a barred related care provider
Fact.Description:
The dollars of this filer's own care expenses (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) that the filer paid to a care provider barred by IRC 21(e)(6) — the filer's spouse, the parent of the qualifying child, a person the filer or spouse can claim as a dependent, or the filer's own child who had not reached age 19 by the close of the year.
QUESTION TEXT: "You told us one of your care providers is someone the credit does not allow you to pay. How much of the care expenses you entered for yourself did you pay to that provider?" (enter 0 if none of them).
HELP TEXT: the printed caution is the whole of the rule — "Don't list an ineligible related individual as a care provider on line 1. No credit is allowed for any amount paid to your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by the end of the year and they can't be your dependent" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3).
WHY THE QUESTION HANGS HERE AND NOT ON THE PROVIDER. The provider collection already carries a per-provider amount (cdcc:/cdccCareProviders/*/amountPaidForCare) but no link saying WHICH qualifying person that payment bought care for, and a provider's payment can also contain dollars that are not in the credit at all (care in another year, care that is not employment-related). Subtracting a provider's gross payment from an arbitrary person's expenses would remove allowed dollars; asking the allocation per person removes exactly the disallowed ones. This is shape (ii) of the two the rebody contract at cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider offered, chosen on the record for that reason.
ASKED WHEN: the return reports at least one barred provider (cdcc:/cdccCareProviders/*/writableIsBarredRelatedProvider true on some row) and this filer has qualifying expenses (../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses).
UNANSWERED: on that population the return is REFUSED (cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider), which is the narrowed residue of the refusal that used to fire on every barred provider whether or not anything could be netted. Nothing is defaulted: a $0 default would let the disallowed dollars stay inside the credit silently. Where no provider is barred the question is never asked and nothing is subtracted.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount, not less than $0. An answer larger than the expense it is taken out of is floored rather than refused — the netted amount never goes below $0 — because over-answering can only reduce the credit, which is the taxpayer-adverse direction.
FEEDS: subtracted from ../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount inside ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is Form 2441 line 2 column (d). Because the subtraction lands in that wrapper rather than in the credit total, it reaches the more-than-three RANKING as well as the printed rows, line 3 and line 30: the person whose expenses were mostly paid to a barred provider stops out-ranking a person whose were not.

Fact.Name: Care expenses also included in Schedule A medical expenses
Fact.Description:
The dollars of this filer's care expenses (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) that the filer ALSO included in the medical expenses on Schedule A line 1.
QUESTION TEXT: "Did you include any of these care expenses in your medical expenses on Schedule A? If so, how much?" (enter 0 if none).
HELP TEXT: "You can't use the same expenses to claim both a credit and a medical expense deduction" (Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 10; Instructions for Form 2441, lines 124-130). Enter the part of the care expenses you entered for this person that is also in your Schedule A medical expenses; it is taken out of the expenses used for the credit. If your care expenses are more than the credit's limit (the dollar limit, $3,000 for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more, or your earned income if that is smaller), you can put the excess on Schedule A without lowering the credit; if you put all of them on Schedule A, none of them can be used for the credit (Pub. 503 lines 693-698).
ASKED WHEN: this filer is a qualifying person for the credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson: a spouse physically or mentally unable to care for themselves), AND the filer paid qualifying care expenses (../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses), AND the return itemizes deductions (taxCalculations:/wantsStandardDeduction false: Schedule A is claimed and either exceeds the standard deduction or the filer elects to itemize; Form 2441 instructions lines 124-126: medical expenses "if you itemize deductions on Schedule A") AND Schedule A has medical expenses (scheduleA:/allowableMedicalExpenses more than $0).
UNANSWERED: on that population this person's line 2 column (d) amount (../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) and the credit are Incomplete; everywhere else it is not asked and nothing is subtracted.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount, not less than $0; the netted amount never goes below $0.
FEEDS: subtracted from ../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount inside ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is line 2 column (d), and so line 3 and line 30. Schedule A itself does not change: the answer is dollars the filer kept in Schedule A line 1. Care expenses that are also medical expenses can be used "either way, but you can't use the same expenses to claim both a credit and a medical expense deduction" (Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 10), so the filer's Schedule A entry is taken as that choice and those dollars leave the credit. IRC 213(e) is the statute's one-use rule: an expense allowed as the credit is not treated as a medical expense.

Fact.Name: Qualifying Expense Amount for CDCC
Fact.Description:
Form 2441 line 2 column (d) for a filer who is a qualifying person (a spouse physically or mentally unable to care for themselves who lived with the filer more than half of 2025): the qualified expenses both incurred AND paid in 2025 for this filer's care, less any part a state social services agency reimbursed.
QUESTION TEXT: "How much did you pay in 2025 for care this person received in 2025? Don't include any amount a state social services agency paid you back."
HELP TEXT: Expenses a state social services agency reimburses aren't qualified expenses, so enter what you paid minus what the agency reimbursed (i2441 lines 73-74; Pub. 503 lines 679-682). Example (Pub. 503 lines 683-685): you paid $3,000 for this person's care and a state social services agency reimbursed you $2,000; enter $1,000. The amount you paid each care provider (Form 2441 line 1 column (e)) is asked separately and is NOT reduced by any reimbursement (i2441 lines 153-157, right column).
HELP TEXT, THE WORK-RELATED PART: "Enter only what you paid so that you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) could work or look for work. If a payment was partly for care that let you work and partly for something else, enter only the work-related part - you don't have to split it if only a small part was for something else. If you worked or looked for work for only part of the time the care covered, count only the care for that part: for example, $250 a month all year while you worked only 2 1/2 months is $625. If you work part-time, count care for the days you worked (a day with at least 1 hour of work is a work day) - unless the provider charges by the week or month whatever days you use, in which case the whole charge can count. Unpaid volunteer work is not work." (Pub. 503 lines 408-440 and 508-513; IRC 21(b)(2)(A).)
HELP TEXT, HOUSEHOLD SERVICES: "You can include what you paid for household services - a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper or cleaning person - if the services were at least partly for the care of this person. Don't include a chauffeur, bartender or gardener." (Pub. 503 lines 489-500, right column.)
The 13th-birthday rule on the dependent twin (familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) does not reach this fact: a filer is a qualifying person only as a spouse unable to care for themselves, not as a child under 13.
TIMING — the amount asked for is care INCURRED in 2025 and PAID in 2025. Three kinds of expense do not belong in it (Form 2441's own caution above line 2, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, pages 3-4): • care this person received in 2024 that you did not pay for until 2025. Enter those on the separate 2024-expenses-paid-in-2025 question (cdcc:/writableCdccPriorYearExpensesPaidInCurrentYear); they reach the credit through Worksheet A and Form 2441 line 9b, so entering them here as well claims the same dollars twice — once through line 3 and again through line 9b; • care received in 2025 that you will not pay for until 2026. Those may increase your 2026 credit instead; • care you prepaid in 2025 for care to be provided in 2026. Those can only be used to figure your 2026 credit.
NOT CARE — leave these out of the amount (i2441 lines 115-123; Pub. 503 lines 443-470): • an OVERNIGHT camp. No amount paid for services outside your household at a camp where this person stays overnight is a qualified expense (IRC 21(b)(2)(A), closing sentence). A DAY camp does count, even one that specializes in an activity such as computers or soccer; • schooling at the kindergarten level or above, summer school, and tutoring programs. Nursery school, preschool and similar programs BELOW the kindergarten level ARE care, and so is before- or after-school care of a child in kindergarten or a higher grade; • food, lodging, clothing, education and entertainment, unless the amount is incidental to the care and cannot be separated from the cost of the care.
BENEFITS — if you received dependent care benefits from an employer's plan, don't include care that was paid for with the benefits that were EXCLUDED FROM YOUR INCOME (Form 2441 line 28, cdcc:/cdccSumOfDeductibleAndExcludedBenefitsAmount). Care you paid for with benefits that were TAXABLE to you (Form 2441 line 26) does count — those dollars are wages. The total you leave out across all of the persons on this return should not exceed line 28. This is what Form 2441 line 30 means by "Don't include in column (d) any benefits shown on line 28 above." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 2; 2025 Instructions for Form 2441, Column (d), "If you completed Part III, don't include in column (d) any benefits shown on line 28.", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3). THE GRAPH DOES NOT ASK A SECOND TIME AND DOES NOT SUBTRACT LINE 28 FOR YOU: the total qualified expenses question (Form 2441 line 16, cdcc:/writableCdccTotalQualifiedDependentCareExpenses) is the GROSS figure that DOES include employer-covered care, and this question is the net one. Line 16 also counts expenses you INCURRED in 2025 whenever paid ("It doesn't matter when the expenses were paid", i2441 lines 375-377), so line 16 minus line 28 is not this amount and cannot be used to derive it.
ASKED WHEN: this filer is a qualifying person for the credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson) and ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is true.
UNANSWERED: stays unanswered; ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount and the credit are Incomplete, never a default.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount.
FEEDS: ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is line 2 column (d); its sum with the other qualifying persons' amounts is line 3 before the dollar limit, and line 30 on a Part III return.

Fact.Name: Some of this person's care was provided outside your home
Fact.Description:
Whether any part of the care COVERED BY THE AMOUNT ENTERED for this person (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, Form 2441 column (d)) was provided OUTSIDE the taxpayer's household.
QUESTION TEXT: "Was any of the care included in the amount you entered for this person provided somewhere other than your home?"
SCOPED TO THE AMOUNT, DELIBERATELY, rather than to the person's care in the abstract ("Was any of this person's care provided somewhere other than your home?"): worded that way, nothing the filer could honestly do would clear cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest, because that refusal reads no dollar, so reducing the amount to the in-home part — the remedy the knockout's own Description promises — would change none of the flag's conjuncts, leaving only the falsely-answered exit. Scoped to the amount, the promised remedy works as written: a filer who leaves the out-of-home dollars out of column (d) answers No truthfully, the 8-hour question below is never reached, and the refusal clears.
HELP TEXT: Care at a daycare centre, a day camp, a relative's house or anywhere else that is not your home is care provided outside your home. Care given in your home by a babysitter, nanny or housekeeper is not. Answer about the amount you just entered, not about the person's whole year. Why it is asked: for a person who is NOT your dependent child under 13, care outside your home counts toward the credit only if that person regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home ("You can include the cost of care provided outside your home for your dependent under age 13, or any other qualifying person who regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 2; Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 7). If this person does not regularly spend 8 hours a day in your home, go back and enter only what you paid for care given IN your home — then the answer here is No.
ASKED WHEN: this filer is a qualifying person for the credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson) and ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is true. A filer who is a qualifying person is always the IRC 21(b)(1)(C) incapacitated spouse — never the paragraph (1)(A) under-13 dependent — so the 8-hour test always applies here and there is no limb to exclude. The expenses conjunct is IN ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest's own All, IsComplete-guarded — a filer with no qualifying expenses contributes $0 to the credit and is never refused over where their care happened.
UNANSWERED: nothing refuses and nothing is Incomplete — cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest is IsComplete-first and resolves false, exactly as cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider does for its own attestation (ruling 6: a question the filer never reached never refuses). The application must carry this as a required screen on the person's care card.
VALIDATION: Boolean, Yes / No.
FEEDS: ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest, and through it cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest.

Fact.Name: This person regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home
Fact.Description:
Whether this qualifying person regularly spends at least 8 hours EACH DAY in the taxpayer's household — IRC 21(b)(2)(B)(ii)'s test for counting care given outside the home.
QUESTION TEXT: "Does this person regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in your home?"
HELP TEXT: This is about the person, not about the care. It is the test that decides whether the care you paid for outside your home counts toward the credit at all ("any other qualifying person who regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 2; Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 7). If the answer is No, go back and take the amounts you paid for care given outside your home out of this person's care expenses — only care given IN your home counts for them — and the previous question, which asks about the amount you entered, then becomes a truthful No.
ASKED WHEN: ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold is true. Not asked otherwise: the test only decides whether OUT-OF-HOME care can be counted.
UNANSWERED: nothing refuses and nothing is Incomplete — see ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold's UNANSWERED note; the refusal is IsComplete-first.
VALIDATION: Boolean, Yes / No.
FEEDS: ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest, and through it cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest.

Fact.Name: Out-of-home care for a person who fails the 8-hour test
Fact.Description:
This filer is a qualifying person (the IRC 21(b)(1)(C) incapacitated spouse, never an under-13 dependent), some of their care was given outside the taxpayer's home, and they do not regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in that home — so IRC 21(b)(2)(B) does not let the out-of-home part of their expenses be taken into account. Complete-safe: false whenever either attestation is unanswered.
THE EXPENSES CONJUNCT. ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is read here, IsComplete-guarded like its siblings, so a filer the return claims no care expenses for is never refused over where their care happened: their column (d) contribution is $0 and no disallowed dollar can reach the credit through them. Without the guard the unanswered-expense path would go Incomplete rather than false. Note the location attestation is scoped to the AMOUNT ENTERED, not to the person's care in the abstract — that is what makes this refusal correctable, see ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold's own Description.
